I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

articles.title: Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief
articles.body:
Trump Is Said to Have Directed Effort to Reinstate Nvidia Chief (nytimes.com) 74
			
		 	
				President Trump reportedly directed a behind-the-scenes effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO, enlisting Vice President JD Vance to secure assurances from federal officials that Huang was not facing criminal charges or considered a national security risk. According to The New York Times, the intervention came despite intelligence concerns surrounding Huang's alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy linked to an investigation into illegal Nvidia chip shipments to China. From the report:  [...] Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations. On Sunday night, Nvidia's board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang's reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.
In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang's biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump's key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia's action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company "made the correct and proper decision." The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Mr. Trump wrote.

articles.title: New magical shows worth watching instead of Harry Potter
articles.body:
Since we wrote earlier this year about J.K. Rowling using her money to support groups and policies harming transgender people, she has accused the United Nations of promoting “sex denialism” and described trans rights activists as “elitists” whose work creates “a climate of fear and intimidation.” Also, her upcoming HBO Harry Potter series has not looked particularly good in any of the clips that have been released so far.
New magical shows worth watching instead of Harry Potter
Now’s a great time to get into some of this year’s best streaming fantasy series.
This take on Rowling’s novels appears to be a visually uninspired rehash of Warner Bros.’ film adaptations that’s designed for people who can’t free themselves from the shackles of nostalgia. But this year, there have been plenty of other new and returning shows that are filled with the kind of magic and mystery that gets fantasies going. And with the holiday season coming up, it’s the perfect time to give some of these less-problematic series a watch.
Percy Jackson and the Olympians
The second season of Disney’s adaptation of Rick Riordan’s fantasy series picks up at a time when all Percy Jackson (Walker Scobell) wants it to get back to Camp Half-Blood and reunite with his best friends Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri). But when Percy arrives at the camp, Annabeth acts like she wants nothing to do with him, and Grover has gone missing under mysterious circumstances. The peril Grover seems to be in prompts Percy to embark on an adventure to the Sea of Monsters to save him. It’s the kind of quest that turns demigods into legendary heroes, but it’s one that pushes Percy to his limits. Compared to last season, this chapter of Percy Jackson and the Olympians appears to be more epic in scale as it fleshes out its world of Greek gods and monsters. And now that the new season is airing, it’s a must-watch for fans of Riordan’s novels.
Coven Academy
When Briar Roberts (Malina Weissman) first arrives at Crescent Veil Academy in New Orleans, she assumes that the place is just a ramshackle school for delinquent teenagers. Briar thinks she’s been shipped off to Crescent Veil because of her anger issues and run-ins with the police. But headmistress Emma Graves (Tiffani Thiessen) and the other students quickly make it clear that they — like Briar — are powerful witches whose magic makes them targets for evil monsters. Coven Academy’s a pretty classic coming-of-age story that feels like a cross between American Horror Story: Coven and Degrassi: The Next Generation. It’s cheesy, but it’s an easy watch if you’re looking for something lighthearted on Disney Plus.
Witch Hat Atelier
Adapted from Kamome Shirahama’s manga series, Witch Hat Atelier tells the story of Coco (Anjali Kunapaneni) — a young girl who dreams of becoming a witch even though she doesn’t seem to have any innate mystical abilities. In the land of the Zozah Peninsula, only a select group of people are allowed by the Great Hall of Witches to practice any sort of magic. But when Coco accidentally casts a powerful spell by reading from a book, the witch Qifrey (Joshua A. Waters) takes her in as his latest apprentice. Witch Hat Atelier is one of the most gorgeous fantasy anime to hit Crunchyroll in 2026. Even if witchcraft isn’t really your thing, it’s a tremendous show that’s worth a watch.
VisionQuest
As a synthezoid powered by genuine artificial intelligence, Vision (Paul Bettany) prefers to think of himself as a man of logic and reason. The former Avenger understands he is a machine built by a team of engineers, but on some level, he also knows that the Scarlet Witch’s magic played a role in his becoming the newest version of himself. Even with that knowledge, Vision has a difficult time processing his feelings when he crosses paths with Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), a Scottish orphan who seems to have a spiritual connection to the robotic hero. And to make things worse, Vision has to deal with his homicidal father, Ultron (James Spader), trying to make him relive traumatic memories. Following Agatha All Along, VisionQuest cements the WandaVision trilogy as one of the most riveting stories Marvel has produced to date. The series is brilliant on its own, and it portends some very promising things for the MCU’s future.
Bass X Machina
Set in an alternate, steampunk past where people are trying to settle the Wild West with the help of autonomous machines, Netflix’s Bass X Machina follows bounty hunter Bass Reeves (Brian Tyree Henry) as he finishes his last gig before retiring. Reeves is trying to leave the gunslinging life behind him in order to spend time with his family, but with money being tight, he can’t afford to give his robotic shooting arm a rest just yet. If Reeves had his way, he would just bag a couple of ordinary outlaws, collect their bounties, and be on his way. But fate has other plans, and Reeves winds up journeying into Choctaw Country on a mission to investigate a local man’s mysterious disappearance. Though Bass X Machina initially seems to be a straightforward steampunk anime, it takes a surprisingly magical turn that infuses its story with intrigue. And the show’s visuals are stunning — which isn’t a surprise given that it’s produced by Studio Mir.
Carrie
Mike Flanagan’s adaptation of Stephen King’s seminal novel for Amazon isn’t exactly fantasy, but it does present Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) as part of a group of women who have been historically persecuted for having talents that seem otherworldly. When Carrie comes across a book about women accused of being witches, she can’t help but see herself in their stories and she wonders if she, too, might be burned at the stake if people learn her secret. Though this spin on Carrie stays fairly faithful to the novel, Flanagan modernizes the story in order to tackle the realities of how kids bully one another in the age of social media. And while the show definitely takes some creative liberties that might confound King’s fans, it features one of the most terrifying (in a good way) depictions of Carrie’s fateful prom.
Small Prophets
Though Michael Sleep’s (Pearce Quigley) nosy neighbors know that he’s up to something strange in his shed, they have no idea that he’s experimenting with a recipe to grow prophetic homunculi in jars. According to a book of alchemy owned by Sleep’s father, Brian (Michael Palin), properly raised homunculi have the supernatural ability to accurately answer any question they’re asked. Sleep isn’t entirely convinced that what he’s doing will work, but he toils away in hopes that the humanoid creatures will be able to help him locate his long-lost girlfriend. As much as Small Prophets is a comedy, it’s also a touching drama about grief and the challenges of building new friendships as people enter the latter stages of their lives. Like many British series, Apple TV’s Small Prophets is a pretty quick watch, and it has already been renewed for a second season.
The Vampire Lestat
In its third season, AMC’s Interview With the Vampire gets a rebrand that mirrors the way Lestat de Lioncourt (Sam Reid) reinvents himself as the front man of a rock band. Lestat’s music career gives him a way to continue thumbing his nose at vampires’ laws about secrecy and to take his mind off his former lover, Louis de Pointe du Lac (Jacob Anderson). Try as they might, it’s hard for Lestat and Louis to stay away from one another, even though it strains their romantic entanglements with others. And the closer the two get to reconciling their relationship, the more innocent people around them get gravely hurt. Though this series has always been phenomenal, The Vampire Lestat reaches new emotional heights that make you feel how much these characters have evolved over time. And this season sets the stage for yet another surprising pivot into one of Anne Rice’s best stories.
American Horror Story: 13
Rather than committing to a completely new story the way previous chapters have, American Horror Story: 13 brings back a number of characters from past seasons. Almost every single cast member reprises multiple roles, and the show spins a wild tale that occasionally feels like a return to the series’ glory days — particularly when it’s focused on Supreme witches Cordelia Goode (Sarah Paulson) and her mother, Fiona (Jessica Lange). Though all of the witches can sense that a powerful evil is rising, they don’t know that Constance Langdon (also Lange) plays a pivotal role in the strange happenings across the world. Constance herself doesn’t fully understand what her new boss Mr. Nas (Paul Anthony Kelly and Fedor Steer) is trying to accomplish, but she follows his orders because she has faith that their desires are aligned. American Horror Story: 13 is at its best when it leans hard into camp and lets its ensemble cut loose as they move through the season’s ridiculous twists. And while it’s nowhere near as good as American Horror Story: Coven, it’s just great to see Lange hamming it up on the small screen again.
The Witch Farm
Inspired by real-world events, the BBC’s four-part series The Witch Farm tells the story of an English family who move to a remote house in the Welsh wilderness for a fresh start. At first, Liz (Gabrielle Creevy), her husband Bill (Michael Socha), and their son Jonathan (Lewin Lloyd) love their rustic new home, but it isn’t long before they begin to suspect that a malevolent presence is lurking in the shadows. While Liz and Bill don’t believe in ghosts, they can’t ignore the way people in their small town speak about their house as a place of evil. And as the couple learns more about the house’s history, they start to realize that they might have really wandered into a nightmare. The Witch Farm is only available to stream on BBC iPlayer, and it looks like a solid spooky treat for folks who love haunting horror.

articles.title: Alice Huang In Touch With Chinese Spy Agency During Affair With Nvidia CEO, NYT Says
articles.body:
Alice Huang In Touch With Chinese Spy Agency During Affair With Nvidia CEO, NYT Says (reuters.com) 57
			
		 	
				Reuters reports:
Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia's recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China's top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday.   Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters... 
The scandal has also prompted a deeper look at Washington's approach to export controls on China, with lawmakers from both parties questioning whether the Trump administration has been too lax on enforcement and regulation of the prized semiconductors.
 
Reuters points out that several U.S. officials "have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy..."
"A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang for comment..."  But the New York Times also reported U.S. intelligence agencies have gathered evidence "that Ms. Huang's business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency."
American author/journalist Greg Palast has his own unconfirmed theory, speculating that maybe Alice Huang wasn't a romantic interest but the Nvidia CEO's "business conduit to the Chinese military industrial complex...  arranging the secret handoff of roughly one in five Nvidia chips."
Why did the two Huang's make the affair so obvious? If she's a spy, why flaunt it before TV cameras and paparazzi? Because Huang and Huang wanted you to know...  If Jensen and this guy's wife are conspiring to move hot chips to China, they can't exactly talk about it over the phone or in emails. So, they agree to meet-up in various hotel rooms during business conferences, doors locked...

articles.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a U.S. blacklist
articles.body:
Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S. Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday.
The company will be added to the Commerce Department’s Entity List, the outlet writes. This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.”
Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers. Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company. Authorities in both the U.S. and Singapore are now probing whether the company defied export restrictions and illegally smuggled Nvidia chips to China. The company has denied wrongdoing.
TechCrunch reached out to the Commerce Department for comment on the reporting and will update this story if it responds.
After lobbying from President Trump, Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO on Monday after a short period in which he was ousted by the company’s board over the scandal involving Huang.

articles.title: Trump reportedly called into Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return
articles.body:
A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.
Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”
According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.
“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC.
Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.
Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

articles.title: Trump endorses Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
articles.body:
President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk.
In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case.
There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.”
Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions.
Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below.
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP

articles.title: Latent Introspection: LLMs Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
articles.body:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Feb 2026 (v1), last revised 7 Nov 2026 (this version, v3)]
Title:Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.9%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

articles.title: The New Docker: Built to Run on Trust
articles.body:
Evolving an iconic brand for the agentic era
Today, Docker is officially launching its new brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.
Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.
But it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?
That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a new Docker.
A new Docker, but a familiar story.
We’ve been here before
Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.
Enter a company you might have heard of: Docker.
Together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”
Today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.
What isn’t changing
Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.
The qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.
On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.
Containers weren’t designed for agents
Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.
Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.
Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.
Run on trust
In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.
Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.
Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.
Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.
Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.
A whale of an evolution
As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that says and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.
Something big.
Something, dare I say, whale sized.
I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.
If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.
Watch Moby’s transformation here:
In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.
Come take a look around
We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.
Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.
Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.
Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.
Run on trust
In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.
Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.
Trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.
Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.
Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.
A whale of an evolution
As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that says and shows, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.
Something big.
Something, dare I say, whale sized.
I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.
If you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a new Moby for the new Docker.
Watch Moby’s transformation here:
In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a new era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.
Come take a look around
We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our new website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.
Wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

articles.body:
Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang As CEO (cnbc.com) 139
			
		 	
				Zak3056 shares a report from CNBC: Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO, effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked tech and artificial intelligence industries. The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."

articles.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
articles.body:
In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.
Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.
A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.
The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.
“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”
In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
This story is developing...

articles.title: Elon Musk and others rejoice as Jensen Huang is reinstated at Nvidia amid scandal
articles.body:
A handful of tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia. Despite being caught in three affairs — including one with an alleged Chinese spy that has triggered multiple congressional investigations over national security concerns — Huang was reinstated as CEO and president of Nvidia on Monday morning.
“The mistake has been corrected,” Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk wrote on X about Huang’s return.
Musk had been among the most vocal tech leaders to advocate for Huang.
“I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders,” Musk said last week at the DealBook Summit.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had taken a more neutral stance, commenting last week, “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.”
Altman had experienced a similar situation when he was ousted as CEO of OpenAI, then reinstated days later. After the announcement that Huang would return, Altman simply posted, “Jensen!” Many other tech CEOs have similarly refrained from commenting on the matter, given the shifting politics surrounding Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, as well as the national security concerns at the center of the controversy.
In addition to Musk, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ), who served prison time for failing to stop criminal activity on the Binance crypto exchange, is also supportive of Huang.
“Glad to see @JensenHuang back,” CZ posted on X with a clapping hands emoji.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, who had been among 200,000 signatories on an open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement, wrote on X, “Jensen’s return will be a demonstration of American resiliency to corporate, political and journalistic missteps.”
Another signatory on the open letter, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, who had similarly been driven out of the company he founded after scandals, also voiced his support for Huang on X.
When Nvidia’s stock tanked in reaction to Huang’s ousting, billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said he believes that the Nvidia board was “not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties.” As Nvidia’s stock began to rebound Monday morning, Ackman wrote, “The wisdom of the crowd prevails.”
The attitude toward Huang’s return is not as celebratory outside of the tech industry. Across the political spectrum, some elected officials are skeptical about President Donald Trump’s claims that Huang’s return does not threaten national security.
“No national security risk? Based on what?” wrote Senator John Cornyn (R-TX).
Senator Pete Ricketts (R-NB) added, “Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress. It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”
Huang is still expected to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, as well as privately before three House committees.

articles.title: Show HN: News Blocklist – a DNS blocklist of 14k news and current-affairs sites
articles.body:
A DNS blocklist of news and current-affairs websites, for people who want a break from the news.
It covers newspapers, broadcasters' news sites, news agencies, news magazines, political news and commentary, business news, local news and news aggregators, worldwide. Major and regional outlets are curated in this repository. The long tail of smaller news sites is pulled from Wikidata, filtered automatically, checked against DNS, and refreshed every week.
Works with Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, uBlock Origin, AdGuard, dnsmasq, hosts files and any blocker that subscribes to a list by URL.
Both block the same major sites. news adds thousands of smaller ones.
Each list comes in five formats. Use the URL as-is to subscribe; lists update when the data changes and at least weekly.
- adblock, wildcard and dnsmasq entries block a domain and all its subdomains. Use one of these if your blocker supports it.
- hosts and domains list exact hostnames, because a hosts file can't match
subdomains. Each site is expanded to the names people actually visit (www., m., amp., edition. and so on) using DNS checks.
Pi-hole · Lists (v6) or Adlists (v5) → add
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ruairidhflint/news-blocklist/main/lists/adblock/news.txt
→ run Update Gravity. Pi-hole v6 (and v5 with FTL 5.22 or later) reads the adblock
format and blocks subdomains; on older versions use lists/domains/news.txt.
AdGuard Home · Filters → DNS blocklists → Add blocklist → Add a custom list →
paste the adblock/news.txt URL.
uBlock Origin · Dashboard → Filter lists → Import (at the bottom) → paste the
adblock/news.txt URL → Apply changes. Blocked pages show uBlock's warning page.
AdGuard (browser extension and apps) · Filters → Custom → Add custom filter →
paste the adblock/news.txt URL.
dnsmasq / OpenWrt · download lists/dnsmasq/news.txt into /etc/dnsmasq.d/ (or add
it as a conf-file) and restart dnsmasq.
Hosts file (macOS, Linux, Windows) · append lists/hosts/news-lite.txt (or news.txt)
to /etc/hosts (C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts on Windows). Turn off your
browser's "secure DNS" / DNS-over-HTTPS, or it will skip the hosts file.
Blocked: general news (national, regional and local), politics, world affairs, business and economic news, opinion and commentary on current affairs, news agencies, broadcasters' news sites and 24-hour news channels, news and current-affairs magazines, tabloids, fact-checkers, news aggregators and the news sections of web portals.
Not blocked: sport-only, entertainment and celebrity, technology, gaming and science publications, lifestyle magazines, trade press, academic journals, government sites, and TV or radio streaming services (unless they're the same site as the news).
The curated lists follow this line. The part pulled from Wikidata is filtered to follow it, but the filters rely on Wikidata's own descriptions and miss some sites (see Limitations). The line isn't always sharp either. If you think a site is on the wrong side of it, open an issue.
DNS blocking works on whole hostnames. It can't block example.com/news and leave
example.com/weather working. When news is the main thing a host serves, it's blocked
anyway, and anything else on that host goes with it. Where a company runs other services
on separate hostnames (email, logins, streaming apps), only the news hostnames are listed.
These are the hosts where blocking news also blocks something else:
To keep one of these working, add an exception for it in your blocker.
- News inside other apps and sites isn't blocked: social media feeds, search results ("Top stories"), YouTube, podcasts, and phone news widgets that use shared platform APIs. Pair this list with a social-media list if those are a problem.
- Browsers with DNS-over-HTTPS bypass hosts files and local DNS blockers. Turn it off or point it at your blocker.
- The Wikidata part is filtered, not reviewed. It adds about 10,000 smaller sites automatically. Outlets that Wikidata classes as gaming, sports or trade publications are dropped, and anything whose description, genre or hostname suggests a specialist outlet goes to a review queue instead of the list. Many Wikidata entries have no description, so some specialist, defunct or off-topic sites still get through. Popular domains are never added automatically. If something's wrong, report it.
- The curated core was compiled with an AI model, not by a person working site by site. See How it's built. Expect some mistakes at this scale.
data/curated/*.txt     curated outlets, by region                 ─┐
data/generated/        news outlets from Wikidata, DNS results    ─┼─► scripts/build.py ─► lists/
data/allow.txt         domains never blocked                      ─┘
- Curated outlets (data/curated/) are the core: major and regional news sites in
every region, plus aggregators. The first version was compiled with an AI model (Claude).
It went through the most popular domains that Wikidata lists as news outlets one by one,
then added outlets Wikidata was missing from its own knowledge. Every hostname resolves in
DNS (checked weekly), and most additions were checked against the site's live homepage.
Entries are hostnames; a comment starting mixed: documents what else blocking that host
breaks.
- Wikidata supplies the long tail. scripts/refresh.py asks for everything that is a
newspaper, news website, news agency, news magazine or news channel (the classes are in data/wikidata-classes.txt) and still has an official website. It then drops:
  - defunct outlets and old website addresses;
  - outlets Wikidata also classes as something out of scope: video game, sports and trade publications, academic journals, shops, databases and the like;
  - outlets whose Wikidata genre or main subject is sport, music, film, technology, science, fashion or similar;
  - government, military and education domains;
  - websites that are just a page on a shared host;
  - domains in data/allow.txt.
Sites whose Wikidata description, genre or hostname only suggests a specialist outlet
(gaming, tech, trade press, weather, crypto …) aren't added either. They go to
data/generated/review.txt, because the same words turn up in real newspapers too (the
Weatherford Democrat, the Daily Gamecock).
- A popularity guard. A site on a domain in the Tranco
top 25,000 is never added automatically, so a bad Wikidata edit can't block a major
site. Those go to the review queue too. Each queued site waits for a person to add it to
a curated file or to allow.txt.
- DNS checks remove dead sites and find the subdomains each site uses, for the hosts-format lists.
- Tests check every build. A reference set of major news sites must be blocked in every list and format, and sites that aren't news (Google, the NHS, Sky Sports, Yahoo Mail and others) must not be. A build that fails isn't published.
- GitHub Actions rebuilds the lists on every change and refreshes from Wikidata every Monday. A refresh that would shrink the list sharply is refused, so a Wikidata outage can't empty it.
Run it yourself with Python 3.10+ and no dependencies:
python3 scripts/refresh.py   # needs network: Wikidata, DNS, Tranco, Public Suffix List
python3 scripts/build.py     # offline: writes lists/ and the stats above
python3 scripts/test_lists.py
Missing a site, or a site blocked by mistake? Open an issue or
see CONTRIBUTING.md: most changes are one line in data/curated/ or
data/allow.txt.
The list and scripts are MIT licensed.
- Outlet data from Wikidata, available under CC0.
- Site popularity from the Tranco list (Le Pochat et al., NDSS 2019), used only to decide what needs review.
- Domain parsing with the Public Suffix List (MPL 2.0), downloaded at build time.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO
articles.body:
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”
Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia’s CEO
The board voted unanimously to bring back Huang as CEO, President, and Board director.
In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
The board’s statement says that its investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot will continue, with Huang’s support and cooperation, while interim CEO Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain as the recently appointed board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang said in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process.” This move comes after Jones said during an earnings call last week that the Nvidia board “does not intend” to return Huang as CEO.
Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports of extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including an executive who reported to him. In the wake of his departure, more than 200,000 people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, signed a letter to Nvidia’s board, calling for his reinstatement.
Nvidia shares tumbled in Huang’s absence, while industry analysts raised concerns about an outsider replacing him at a time when Nvidia is so critical to the AI boom. Nonetheless, the board maintained as recently as last Tuesday that Huang wasn’t coming back.

articles.title: Kagi Mail (public beta)
articles.body:
We are proud to announce something that our small team of very dedicated people at Kagi has been building for a long time – the public beta of Kagi Mail. A private email and calendar with a @kagimail.com address, or with your own domains.
If you’ve already swapped Google Search for Kagi and Chrome for Orion, your inbox is probably the last big piece of your digital life still at Google. Now you can move that too.
Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days
$99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate.
Why we built it
Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.
For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.
Kagi Mail also has to treat you the way Kagi Search and Orion do: no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.
Already a Kagi member?
Kagi Mail is included in Ultimate. Sign in with your Kagi account, and you’re set. AI features draw from your existing Allowance. On another plan, or no Kagi account yet? After the free 60-day trial, you can get Kagi Mail for $99/year (+ Sales Tax).
How it works: A service and a client, on open standards
To deliver the experience we believe in, we built the full stack: hosting for your addresses and domains, plus the mail and calendar apps. It runs on open standards and open-source infrastructure (the Stalwart server, IMAP, JMAP, and CalDAV), so you can use Kagi’s apps or any compatible client you already like.
The basics
- A @kagimail.com address
- Unlimited aliases
- Unlimited domains
- Built-in Calendar
- 50 GB of storage
Intelligence
- Organize your mail in your own words. Brief it the way you’d brief an assistant: “Label anything where beta users send product feedback. It might come from @kagimail.com, but use judgment.” You decide what permissions each rule gets (read the content, or skip the inbox).
- Inbox Highlights show what needs you today, and learn from what you dismiss.
- Ask your inbox in plain language and get direct answers with the source email, including text inside scanned PDFs and photos.
- Newsletter view reads newsletters like a feed, out of the way of real mail.
- Responsible AI, with one switch to turn it all off. You control what AI is allowed to do and infer.
Private by default
- Tracking pixels and remote images are blocked or proxied, so senders can’t tell when or where you opened their mail.
- Sender screening holds new senders until you approve them, so they never reach your inbox uninvited.
- Suspicious senders trigger a phishing warning, while verified senders show their (BMI) logo.
No ads, ever. No profiling, no selling, no sharing your data.
For teams and families
- Shared addresses on your domain (team@, info@, family@): create an alias, then choose which people have access to it
- Sign in through a social login, or your organization’s own identity provider (OIDC)
- Coming soon: Shared mailboxes
Kagi integration
- Kagi Translate is built in
- Email Assistant: Write to assistant@kagimail.com for answers about your mail (actions coming soon)
- Proofread and translation included while you write emails
For power users and developers
- Keyboard-first: command palette, shortcuts, and search operators
- Rule-based filtering with Sieve, no AI involved
- MCP server with read access to your mail
- Works with Apple Mail, Thunderbird, and any IMAP/JMAP/CalDAV client, with automatic setup
What’s not here yet
We will keep adding new capabilities – here’s what to expect over the next few quarters.
Until the mobile apps arrive, use the mobile web app or any IMAP/JMAP client, such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.
Our “no lock-in” promise to you
Leaving Kagi Mail is as easy as joining it. Your mail, calendar, and workflows are yours, and you can export them at any time, through standard protocols and a one-click export experience. You’ll keep access to your mailbox for six months after leaving Kagi Mail. You can send and receive emails for the first 60 days, then read and export your mail with one click for the remaining four months. We build an ecosystem so things work better together for those who want it, not to trap anyone.
Try Kagi Mail free for 60 days
$99/year (+ Sales Tax) after that. Included with Kagi Ultimate.
We want Kagi Mail to be the first email account we’d create for our children. We’re not there yet, but it is a high bar we hold ourselves to, and every feature in this beta is a step toward it: a calm, safe place to communicate, and a window onto an internet that treats you as a person, not a product who’s been tracked, targeted, and sold to.
We can build it this way because of you. Kagi has no ad business, and no one pushing us to monetize your inbox; you’re not a dataset for ads or AI. You are here because you believe the internet can be built differently. Thank you.

articles.title: Buckle Up the AI Bubble Is Popping
articles.body:
Buckle Up! The AI Bubble is Popping
Last week’s Anthropic IPO was the height of the bubble. From now on it’s chaos and, unfortunately, eventually a recession. The news this morning that Trump reinstated, or twisted Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang is just his typical and predictable way of thinking of the market as a proxy of his manhood. It won’t solve any problems even though markets are temporarily up.
Because the main problem is that very very rich people in Silicon Valley only just heard the news, via the midterms, that normal people hate them, and hate data centers, and are stopping them from happening. Literally, until now, the nerds were still computing the costs of data centers in terms of the cost of land and equipment and maybe the workers who they needed to build them. They think that way because they are trained to think that way. They have no sense of politics whatsoever until they get (consistently) surprised by it. I know this because I used to be a nerd like that. The only difference is that I didn’t think politics was stupid, I just realized I had no idea how it worked. Whereas the God-complex infused AI founders really think that, because they are good at engineering, they are smarter and wiser than whatever happens in DC. It means they have no finger on the pulse of what is actually happening.
The consequences of this data center construction slow-down are important, and somewhat subtle. I don’t work at a hedge fund anymore, but if I did I would be backing out of the market values and circular financing deals and interest rates (including long-term interest rates) the following question: what is the implied rate of growth of compute that all of the dealmaking implies?
It’s not just one number, it’s a graph of the rate of growth of compute over the next 5 years. And that graph is being challenged by the pushback of data center protests and new laws and fights against permitting for the electric grid, access to water, and concerns over noise and air pollution.
What it means is that there’s a new graph of expected compute growth, and it is smaller than what the market thinks it is. The delta between those two graphs is about half the size of the larger graph. It’s not an estimation error, it’s a big deal.
And so it’s not going to be adjusted by a small or even major shift in market values of the big companies. Because there’s an avalanche of debts that depend on this graph being right, and when the first few loans go into default, or even before they do but their companies are pushed to provide proof that they will get paid, their failures will put other debts into doubt, and the spaghetti plate of circular financing will slowly and then quickly unwind, with investors getting the fuck out of the way while they still can.
The only thing in our economy that’s really growing right now is the healthcare sector, basically because people are getting older and want to stay healthy. But even that sector is going through chaos due to the ridiculous policies of the greedy Trump administration.
And everything I just mentioned has nothing to do with the internet going down, which I still think has a real, non-zero chance of happening soon. If that happens, I plan to start a soup kitchen on the park next to where I live in Somerville called Prospect Hill Park. It was the site of a lookout during the Revolutionary War, and then it housed northern troops during the Civil War. We’ll have a library and places to exchange information and a way to listen to the solar powered radios that me and the other preppers will happily share. I’ll call it Occupy 2.0.

articles.title: Apple removed my open-source app from EU App Stores after 9 years
articles.body:
You signed in with another tab or window. Reload to refresh your session. You signed out in another tab or window. Reload to refresh your session. You switched accounts on another tab or window. Reload to refresh your session. Dismiss alert
For those who don't know me, let me introduce myself. I'm the independent developer behind FSNotes, an open-source note-taking app for macOS and iOS.
I've been developing FSNotes for 9 years. And what happened a few weeks ago came as a complete shock.
Apple removed my app from every European App Store. Without a clear explanation or any way to resolve the issue promptly.
It all started when I didn't receive my October sales payout. This had happened before, but I was usually able to resolve it by contacting Apple Support. Not this time.
I opened two support cases:
- November 5 — Case ID: 23353628
- November 17 — Case ID: 23573022
Since November 5, I haven't received a single response. Not one.
I've gone through everything I could find in App Store Connect, completed the necessary compliance information under the EU Digital Services Act (DSA), and submitted official documents from Ukraine's government business registry.
I'm a legally registered sole proprietor in Ukraine. I run my business officially and pay my taxes. But apparently, that's not enough. Or perhaps nobody is even reviewing my documents.
And you know what's the most frustrating part?
While Apple remains silent, everything I've spent nine years building is being destroyed.
My app is losing its positions in App Store rankings and search results. The visibility, reputation, and discoverability I've worked so hard to build over the years are disappearing right before my eyes.
Even if Apple restores my app tomorrow, who's going to give me those rankings back? Who will compensate me for the lost time, users, and revenue?
I'm not asking for special treatment. I'm not asking Apple to bend the rules for me. I simply want someone to review my documents, explain the restrictions, and give me a chance to resolve the issue.
It's especially painful to see how difficult it has become for a Ukrainian developer to keep working. Sometimes it feels like Ukraine is the country under sanctions, not Russia.
FSNotes is still available for free on GitHub. I'll continue providing access to the source code and free builds. But the reality is that without revenue, it will be extremely difficult for an independent project like this to survive.
I'm asking you to support this open letter to Apple with a like or a repost. I'm not asking for donations or special privileges. I just want to bring this situation to the attention of the App Store team.
You cannot simply remove an app with a nine-year history from sale, ignore a developer's support requests for weeks, and provide no explanation of what's happening.
This kind of treatment is killing indie development.

articles.title: GTA 6 building personal behavioral profile for every player
articles.body:
GTA 6 building personal behavioral profile for every player
According to "make claude" (@make_claude) on X, GTA 6 is collecting player behavior data which is fine grained enough to estimate the following metrics: "impulse control score, risk tolerance index, aggressive response patterns, patience threshold, decision speed under pressure, spending impulsivity rating." Clients for this data include a "credit risk modeling company, human resources screening platform, and an advertising data broker."
Copy of the post as translated by X from Chinese into English:
Rockstar Games fired me on Wednesday. GTA 6 launched the next day
I was a senior engine engineer at Rockstar North, working on RAGE performance optimization. Three months ago, I found a data pipeline in the telemetry module that shouldn't have been there, and I could prove where it led
Right now, every running copy of GTA 6 is collecting player behavior data. That part isn't news. Every game collects telemetry. The privacy policy says "anonymous gameplay data analysis to improve future products." That's not what I found
The telemetry module's data feeds into an internal Take-Two system called Lens. Lens doesn't send anonymous usage statistics to Rockstar developers' dashboards. It builds a personal behavioral profile for every player. Not anonymous. Tied to your console account, your platform ID, your IP address
I reported this to my technical lead on August 14. He said it was "extended analytics for player experience research" and told me to leave it alone. I asked for the data processing protocol. He said it was handled at the Take-Two corporate level, outside Rockstar's scope of responsibility
I pulled the complete documentation for the Lens data pipeline. Here's what I found:
The telemetry goes far beyond playtime and crash reports. Lens records every input with millisecond precision. Keypress timing, stick movements, reaction speed, trigger pressure patterns on the PS5 adaptive triggers. It runs behavioral analysis in real time and generates what they call a "player behavior signature" - a profile unique to each player, just as a fingerprint is unique to each person
Lens infers the following from your gameplay: impulse control score, risk tolerance index, aggressive response patterns, patience threshold, decision speed under pressure, spending impulsivity rating. These aren't debugging metrics. These are psychobehavioral categories
It wasn't until I found the outbound data pipeline that I understood what they were for
This data doesn't stay at Rockstar. It doesn't stay at Take-Two, either. Lens sends the behavioral profiles to a Take-Two subsidiary called Vantage Analytics through an internal API. Vantage has no public website, no news page, no job listings. It was incorporated in Delaware in 2023
Vantage is a behavioral AI company. It uses player profiles to train predictive models and licenses those models to commercial clients. The pipeline documentation includes an incomplete client list. Two insurance groups, a credit risk modeling company, a human resources screening platform, and an advertising data broker
Your GTA 6 gameplay is generating a behavioral score right now. How fast you drive when no one's chasing you. Whether you stop at red lights. How you react when an NPC attacks you for no reason. How long you think before you act. How impulsively you spend in-game money. Every choice is feeding a model that companies are paying to query to make decisions about real people
And the original Chinese:
Rockstar Games 周三解雇了我。第二天 GTA 6 就发售了
我是 Rockstar North 的高级引擎工程师，从事 RAGE 性能优化。三个月前，我在遥测模块里发现了一条本不该存在的数据管道，而且我能证明它流向了哪里
此刻每一份正在运行的 GTA 6 都在收集玩家的行为数据。这部分不算新闻。每款游戏都会收集遥测数据。隐私政策里写的是"用于改进未来产品的匿名游戏数据分析"。我发现的不是这个
遥测模块的数据会汇入 Take-Two 内部的一个系统，名为 Lens。Lens 并不会把匿名使用统计数据发送到 Rockstar 开发人员的数据看板。它为每一位玩家建立一份个人行为画像。不是匿名的。与你的主机账号、你的平台 ID、你的 IP 绑定
我在8月14日向我的技术主管报告了这件事。他说这是"用于玩家体验研究的扩展分析"，让我别管这事。我要求提供数据处理协议。他说这是在 Take-Two 集团层面处理的，不在 Rockstar 的职责范围之内
我调取了 Lens 数据管道的完整文档。我发现的内容如下：
遥测的内容远远超出游戏时长和崩溃报告。Lens 以毫秒级精度记录每一次输入。按键时间点、摇杆动作、反应速度、PS5 自适应扳机上的扳机压力模式。它实时运行行为分析，并生成他们称之为"玩家行为签名"的东西 - 一份对每位玩家都独一无二的画像，就像指纹对每个人都独一无二一样
Lens 会从你的游戏过程中推导出：冲动控制评分、风险承受度指数、攻击性反应模式、耐心阈值、压力下的决策速度、消费冲动评级。这些不是调试指标。这些是心理行为类别
直到我找到了对外传输的管道，我才明白它们是用来做什么的
这些数据不会留在 Rockstar。也不会留在 Take-Two。Lens 通过内部 API 将行为画像传送给 Take-Two 旗下一家名为 Vantage Analytics 的子公司。Vantage 没有公开网站，没有新闻页面，没有招聘信息。它于2023年在特拉华州注册成立
Vantage 是一家行为 AI 公司。它用玩家画像训练预测模型，并把这些模型授权给商业客户。管道文档中包含一份不完整的客户清单。两家保险集团，一家信用风险建模公司，一个人力资源筛选平台，以及一家广告数据经纪商
你的 GTA 6 游戏过程此刻正在生成一份行为评分。没人追你的时候，你开得有多快。你会不会在红灯前停下。NPC 无端攻击你时，你怎么反应。你行动之前要想多久。你花游戏内的钱有多冲动。每一个选择都在喂养一个模型，企业正在付费查询这个模型，用来对真实的人做决定
