articles.title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
articles.body:
Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.
Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.
Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.
And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. Shivon Zilis, who has two children with Musk, also got in on the fun.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle.
Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.
Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke took what one could call a moral stance.
And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one, but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.
Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire also pointed out the obvious market-bending powers of Huang’s reinstatement.
Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?
Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.” In the same appearance, Trump said “we need to protect our geniuses.”
Marc Andreessen didn’t officially comment on the reinstatement, but the a16z cofounder changed his X bio after the news broke. It now reads: “We have to protect our geniuses.”
Trump also seems to be relishing in Huang’s alleged affairs. In another Truth Social post, he superimposed Huang — red bra in hand — into the iconic photo of his reaction to being shot at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.
For Canadian venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, Trump’s intervention is just further proof of Huang’s innocence. Certainly an interesting take!
The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.
Update, November 23rd: This post has been updated with reactions from Shivon Zilis, Tobi Lütke, Shaun Maguire, Chamath Palihapitiya, and Marc Andreessen.

articles.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
articles.body:
US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades (reuters.com) 53
			
		 	
				Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports:  A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course."   Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road."
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."

articles.title: White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
articles.body:
It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”
White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
Trump said Nvidia’s board ‘made the correct and proper decision’ to bring back Jensen Huang.
Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.”
Trump also said, “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
Nvidia said in its announcement that its board “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made them confident reinstating Huang would not pose a national security risk, following reports about his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding:
“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now says that he was calling in to Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument.

articles.title: The AI conversation we're not having
articles.body:
8 Things Two Years in AI Taught Me That Nobody Posts About
AI is threatening everyone. That is the feeling, anyway.
I’ve been working in AI for about two years now. Most recently that’s been at Arcade.dev, helping teams get their agents into real production use. I’m still figuring a lot of it out, like everyone else.
Over these two years, the same questions keep finding me. A friend over dinner wondering if their job is safe. A customer trying to figure out where to even start. Someone new to tech, and someone with decades in it, both quietly asking what actually matters now. I don’t have all the answers, but I’ve collected a few honest ones. Here are eight things I keep coming back to.
1. Do not doubt the skills you already have
What you have built over years is legitimately useful, even if the ground is shifting under it. Your old skill may be transcending into something else. Figure out what that something else is. But do not start by throwing away what you have.
Compounding still works in skills. It is still working.
And you’re not the only one feeling it. Everyone is adjusting to how fast things are moving. Everyone is going through a disruption in their career and their life, and everyone is working hard to get through it. It is not the whole world ending. It is the whole world changing at the same time.
And if you’re just starting out, you have something the rest of us don’t: no baggage. You haven’t spent ten years learning “the right way” to do things that may not matter anymore. Use that. Try the weird idea. Just remember that a fresh idea only counts once you’ve built it.
2. Meet people in person
The digital world is getting weird. More automation, more bots, more noise. So do more of what AI cannot do.
Have food with people. No robot is going to split a pizza with you and ask how your family is doing. Go meet a friend in person and say hello. It opens up perspectives you will never get inside the tech bubble.
That is how I got my job. I met people in person. A LinkedIn profile is a vastly different thing from the person standing in front of you.
3. Your originality is the leverage
There is exactly one person in the world who is like you. No one can replace that. So go after it, big time. I know it is hard. Go after it anyway.
If someone comes after your originality, they have already lost, because they are admitting they do not have their own.
There is always some value you can add in a given situation, regardless of money, title, or anything else. And that value compounds too. Test it.
4. Build something real. Not something fancy.
I see a lot of people talk about agents. Some are even trying to build critical agent infrastructure, and they have not built two agents for themselves.
Building agents is hard. It is not running a prompt. There is deployment, scaling, quality, evals, design, model choice, prompting, cost. Do not underestimate any of it.
If you’re new, this is your edge. Almost every hiring manager will ask the same question: what have you built? So build. Contribute to an open source project. Ship a rough idea. Put something out there that works, even if it’s ugly.
But don’t confuse building with building a lot. Just because you can build something doesn’t mean you should. Knowing what not to build is a skill too. Building what people actually need is vastly different from building something fancy that no one is going to use.
Talk is cheap. Build the right thing.
5. Adoption is slow. Wait for it.
Almost none of this technology has reached real scale yet, outside a few model companies. True adoption happens slowly, because habits are hard to break.
At the end of the day, humans are the consumers of this technology. They pay from their own pockets. They are the economy. AI will take time to make money, and that is exactly where you can make money too, if you are in the industry.
So do not conclude too early. Do not get frustrated. Do not build FOMO. I am not an AI optimist. I am skeptical of many things. But doomsday is not coming either. There will be a place for you to keep adding value.
Wait for habits to break. Wait for people to embrace agents. Wait for people to understand the patterns.
6. Join problem solvers, and ask hard questions
In any industry, look for the people solving a really hard problem. Find that group and join it.
Do not be fooled by a fancy marketing site. In my experience, the people who do not know the depth of building a product end up with the fanciest marketing. The people building great products often do not have time to polish theirs.
So when a company vibes well with you, question it deeply. Who are their customers? How will they sustain long term, financially? How do they make money? If the market crashes, do they have enough funding secured to survive it? What are their case studies? Do they have a sales team?
Ask those questions before you join, not after.
7. Study the past
History repeats itself. That is why we call something a pattern: because it is one.
You have all this fancy AI. Use some of it to study the past. What happened when the internet arrived? When cars were invented? When world wars reshaped everything? You will find clues about what is going to happen to you. Use them as a wedge to reinvent yourself. There is no other choice.
8. Nobody retires from what they love
Billionaires will tell you money will become invalid and nobody will need to work. Regardless of all that, your hard work, your focus, and your perspective are not going away. Your energy is always going to be there. You have to put it on something.
Do not fall for the retire-at-forty trap. Nobody actually retired. Some people made more money. Some stopped working for a company. But nobody ever retired from their passion. Nobody retired from doing the thing they love.
Working for yourself, building something meaningful, that is not going away.
Do something meaningful.
So, who are you going to meet next week? And what agent are you going to build tomorrow?

articles.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
articles.body:
NariQ: Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file, BF16-level on long-horizon agentic tasks
(Nov 20, 2026) We are releasing NariQ v1 GGUFs of Qwen3.8-27B at 3, 2.5 and 2 bits per weight. Run them on our llama.cpp fork (required).
- The 3-bit and 2.5-bit files match BF16 on long-horizon agent tasks, math and image understanding. The 2-bit file scores lower.
- NariQ is a trellis-coded post-training quantization (PTQ), calibrated on real coding-agent traces and stored in a layout that runs on a single GPU.
- More details are in the tech report.
Each cell gives a percentage and a count in parentheses. For DeepSWE, the count is the mean number of fully solved tasks per round. Across the same three rounds, the mean share of each task's new tests that passed was 83.1% (BF16), 82.9% (3-bit), 83.2% (2.5-bit) and 77.2% (2-bit). One BF16 verifier timeout in round 3 counts as zero (338 of 339 trials graded). Each NariQ variant had all 339 trials graded. Terminal-Bench counts solved trials, and the remaining columns count correct answers. The agent runs use the Claude Code CLI (2.1.309, thinking on, effort max) driving the local model, with a 262,144-token context and the model's thinking-mode sampling (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20).
KL divergence from the BF16 model on held-out coding-agent traces, against file size. Every point was measured by us with the same code. Lower is better.
DeepSWE fully solved tasks out of 113, against file size. Our NariQ points and solid BF16 line average three rounds with Claude Code. Our GSQ-RCO points use one round. The hollow diamonds show approximate averages from Unsloth's published Dynamic V3.1 chart (mini-swe-agent). Compare each point with the BF16 line for its harness. Higher is better.
Terminal-Bench 2.1 score over 82 tasks × 3 attempts, against file size. Filled circles are our runs (Claude Code); hollow diamonds are Unsloth's reported results (mini-swe-agent), read from its published Dynamic V3.1 chart (hence ≈; its scores are averages over several passes). The two harnesses differ, so compare each point with the BF16 line of its own harness (solid: ours, dashed: Unsloth's). Higher is better.
Quickstart
One command on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and driver 570 or newer (downloads the fork's binaries and the files, checks them, and fits the context to your GPU):
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp/releases/download/b12431-nariv0/run.sh
bash run.sh 3.0   # or 2.5, 2.0
Or download and serve yourself, with llama-server from the fork:
hf download nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF \
    Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-3.0bpw.gguf Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-mmproj-BF16.gguf --local-dir .
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-3.0bpw.gguf --mmproj Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-mmproj-BF16.gguf \
    -ngl 99 -c 131072 --jinja --port 8080 \
    --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0
The sampling flags are the thinking-mode settings our scores used. -c 131072 fits a 24 GB GPU with little to spare;
lower it if a display shares the GPU, or let run.sh pick the largest context that fits. Use -c 262144 (the model's
full context) on 32 GB or more. GPU memory with the vision projector:
Prebuilt binaries, the Docker image, supported GPUs and build steps: the fork's README.
Decode speed on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell), single session, 512 greedy output tokens, tokens/s:
NariQ on our llama.cpp fork with -fa on -ctk bf16 -ctv bf16 -t 1 -tb 16 --backend-sampling --samplers temperature (greedy sampling on the GPU, BF16 KV cache). UD-IQ3_XXS is Unsloth's file on llama.cpp, measured earlier on the same GPU type.
Known limits and future work
- Requires a NariQ-aware runtime: for now, our llama.cpp fork. Stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio can't load the new tensor types yet; we hope to merge support into upstream llama.cpp. Our internal SGLang plugin and our inference engine built on Resin are a work in progress for potential public release.
- The llama.cpp fork needs more work across hardware. The current fork is focused on SM120 performance (e.g. RTX PRO 6000). Ampere, Ada and Hopper GPUs and Apple M-series GPUs are slower than comparable GGUFs for now; we would love open-source contributions for speedups, as this has been a solo effort. GPUs older than Ampere fall back to slow CPU execution, and AMD and Intel GPUs are not supported yet. GeForce cards have not been tested yet; tested GPUs are RTX PRO 6000, H100, L4 and A10.
- Apple M-series (Metal): build from source; on an M3 Pro (18 GB) decode is about 3.8 tok/s with the 3.0bpw file (4.9 with 2.0bpw), far slower than CUDA. Other Macs are untested.
- The 2-bit file is weaker overall; use the 2.5-bit or 3-bit for higher overall performance.
- The vision tower stays in BF16; only the language model is quantized. The MTP (multi-token prediction) module is not included yet; it is still to be quantized.
- KV-cache and activation quantization are next, so the files fit long contexts on 16 GB consumer GPUs and run faster. Today the KV cache and activations stay in BF16.
Contact us
For technical consulting, compute sponsorships, or partnership inquiries, please contact founders@narilabs.com.
License
These files inherit the base model's Apache-2.0 license; see NOTICE.
Acknowledgements
Thanks to the Qwen team for the amazing Qwen3.8-27B, and to the Unsloth, ExLlamaV3, GSQ-RCO (IST Austria DASLab) and GGML teams, whose open-source work this release builds on. NariQ's trellis codes build on QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024).
Citation
If you use NariQ, please cite the technical report:
@techreport{kim2026nariq,
  title       = {NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks},
  author      = {Doyeob (Toby) Kim},
  institution = {Nari Labs},
  year        = {2026},
  month       = nov,
  eprint      = {2611.26157},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  url         = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26157}
}
Qwen3.8-27B
Following the widespread community adoption of the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 series, we are pleased to introduce Qwen3.8, the most capable generation in the Qwen open-model family to date.
Built on the architectural foundation of Qwen3.5, Qwen3.8 delivers substantial gains across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Qwen3.8-27B brings these advances to a compact, deployment-friendly dense model: a native vision-language model that understands images and videos, with flexible thinking control, designed to carry complex, multi-step tasks through to completion with greater reliability.
Qwen3.8 Highlights
Qwen3.8-27B features the following enhancements:
- Core Capabilities: Comprehensive improvements across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks.
- Agent Execution: Stronger autonomous planning and better handling of environment feedback, leading to more reliable end-to-end task completion.
- Downstream Compatibility: Broader support for popular harnesses and development tools, making it easier to integrate into your existing stack.
- Flexible Thinking Control: Thinking mode is on by default and can be disabled per request; reasoning depth can be tuned with reasoning_effort, and reasoning context from historical messages is retained via preserve_thinking.
- Vision-Language Understanding: Native support for image and video understanding, from STEM diagrams and documents to hour-scale videos.
Model Overview
- Type: Causal Language Model with Vision Encoder
- Training Stage: Pre-training & Post-training
- Language Model
  - Number of Parameters: 27B
  - Hidden Dimension: 5120
  - Token Embedding: 248,320 (Padded)
  - Number of Layers: 64
  - Hidden Layout: 16 × (3 × (Gated DeltaNet → FFN) → 1 × (Gated Attention → FFN))
  - Gated DeltaNet:
    - Number of Linear Attention Heads: 48 for V and 16 for QK
    - Head Dimension: 128
  - Gated Attention:
    - Number of Attention Heads: 24 for Q and 4 for KV
    - Head Dimension: 256
    - Rotary Position Embedding Dimension: 64
  - Feed Forward Network:
    - Intermediate Dimension: 17,408
  - LM Output: 248,320 (Padded)
  - MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): trained with multiple steps
- Context Length: 262,144 natively and extensible up to 1,000,000 tokens.
Best Practices
To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings:
- Sampling Parameters: We suggest using the following sets of sampling parameters: 
  - Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0
  - Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0
 For supported frameworks, you can adjust the presence_penalty parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetition. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance.
- Adequate Output Length: To optimize performance on agentic tasks, we recommend allocating sufficient output length to allow the model to generate detailed and comprehensive responses. For frameworks that support separate token limits for internal reasoning and final outputs, we suggest the following configuration within the 1M context length: 
  - Reasoning Content: Set the maximum output length to 262,144 tokens.
  - Final Response: Set the maximum output length to 131,072 tokens.
These settings provide the necessary capacity for complex reasoning while ensuring ample space for high-quality final deliverables.
- Processing Ultra-Long Texts: Qwen3.8-27B natively supports context lengths of up to 262,144 tokens. For long-horizon tasks where the total length (including both input and output) exceeds this limit, we recommend using RoPE scaling techniques to handle long texts effectively, e.g., YaRN.
- Long Video Understanding: To optimize inference efficiency for plain text and images, the size parameter in the released video_preprocessor_config.json is conservatively configured. It is recommended to set the longest_edge parameter in the video_preprocessor_config file to 469,762,048 (corresponding to 224k video tokens) to enable higher frame-rate sampling for hour-scale videos and thereby achieve superior performance. For example,
{"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}
Alternatively, override the default values via engine startup parameters. For implementation details, refer to: vLLM / SGLang.
Citation
@misc{qwen38,
    title = {{Qwen3.8-Max}: A New Bar for Coding and Cowork},
    url = {https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.8},
    author = {{Qwen Team}},
    month = {August},
    year = {2026}
}
- Downloads last month
  2,243
We're not able to determine the quantization variants.

articles.title: A Partial Evaluator for C
articles.body:
Tempo Specializer - A Partial Evaluator for C
What is Tempo?
Partial evaluation is program
transformation that automates a program
specialization process. Tempo is a
partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various
domains such as operating systems and networking, computer graphics, scientific
computation, software engineering and domain specific languages. A first
workshop on Tempo has been organized in March 1998.
Tempo is now being distributed. Its documentation
is available on line, as well as tutorial
slides.
An Overview of Tempo
Tempo is a partial
evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose
project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI
(France).
Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases:
analysis and specialization.
The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description
of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown.
Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about
known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program,
indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization.
Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase
performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time
analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping
track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers.
Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized
program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs.
Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e.,
source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time
(i.e., run-time binary code generation).
For more details, please consider reading some of our papers, most of which
are available at the following URL: papers.
Program Analysis
As a first step, the user provides a program and specifies what arguments
(including global variables) are static. For example, the user provides
the following code for a miniprintf function, and specifies in
this way that the first argument is static whereas the second is dynamic:
miniprintf(S,D).
miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])
{
  int i = 0;
  while( *fmt != '\0' ) {
    if( *fmt != '%' )
       putchar(*fmt);
    else
      switch(*++fmt) {
        case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;             
        case '%' : putchar('%');     break;
        default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;
      }
    fmt++;
  }
}
From this Tempo produces a program file with analysis annotations.
These annotations can be visualized using colors that highlight the propagation
of the known/unknown information throughout the program.
/*  LEGEND:  STATIC  DYNAMIC
 */
miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])
{
  int i = 0;
  while( *fmt != '\0' ) {
    if( *fmt != '%' )
       putchar(*fmt);
    else
      switch(*++fmt) {
        case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;              
        case '%' : putchar('%');     break;
        default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;
      }
    fmt++;
  }
}
The blue color (bold face for black and white display) represent static
constructions, i.e. values that can be computed at specialization
time. The red color (standard font for black and white display) is for
dynamic expressions, whose value cannot be precomputed knowing only the
static arguments. Basically, everything in blue (bold) will disappear after
specialization; only red (standard font) parts will remain.

on-line partial
evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer

When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user

values must be provided. For example, giving
"<%d,%d>" as the
actual specialization value for the fmt argument of the miniprintf()
function yields the following specialized code.

{
  putchar( '<'    );
  putint ( val[0] );
  putchar( ','    );
  putint ( val[1] );
  putchar( '>'    );
}

specialization values have to be provided.

of the program. In the case of the
miniprintf function, Tempo
generates a runtime specializer rts_miniprintf_1() which can be
used as in the following example.

 * Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format'
 */

...
(*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */
(*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */

can also be generated and used at the same time.

speedups.

Operating system and networking:

Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks,
- 
Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms),
- 
Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries),
-

  - 
Selective broadcast (implicit invocation),

Pattern matching,
  - 
Interpreters,

Software layers,

Generic libraries.

Tempo Specializer - A Partial Evaluator for C
What is Tempo?
Partial evaluation is program
transformation that automates a program
specialization process. Tempo is a
partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various

Tempo is a partial
evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose
project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI
(France).
Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases:
analysis and specialization.
The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description
of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown.
Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about

indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization.
Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase

articles.title: Tesla’s FSD v15 turns driving visuals into Grand Theft Auto
articles.body:
Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system. The centerpiece is Reality View, a real-time generative display that swaps out old wireframe graphics for a live, overhead camera angle that lets drivers see and tap to influence what the car plans to do next.
Tesla’s FSD v15 turns driving visuals into Grand Theft Auto
The update swaps blocky wireframes for a photorealistic overhead feed and promises a “25x” safety boost, even as federal regulators continue investigating the software.
The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently launched just days earlier). Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the update dropped on Saturday.
Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs. By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power. Of course, the update is built for vehicles running Tesla’s newer AI4 (HW4) hardware and upcoming Cybercab platforms, leaving millions of older HW3-equipped cars behind.
Beyond the flashy visuals, v15 packs several practical upgrades. A new Bike Rack Mode lets drivers engage FSD even with hitch accessories attached (though it disables reversing, Summon, and Autopark). The system can now automatically ease off the speed near traffic cameras, with an option to override and permanently mute specific cameras after two cancellations. Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather.
Meanwhile, navigation learns preferred neighborhood routes and favorite parking spots over time, and the cabin camera can now track driver attention through hats and sunglasses while dialing back nagging alerts at higher speeds. Tesla has a pretty poor reputation for ensuring its drivers stay alert while using FSD, so hopefully this upgrade can improve that.
Still, Reality View raises an obvious question: is a hyper-detailed, video-game-style feed on the center touchscreen a helpful window into the car’s “brain,” or a tempting new distraction? For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”.
Tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes. Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.

articles.title: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
articles.body:
Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos.
By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time.
Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money.
As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season.
Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa.
Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context that AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses.
The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context.

articles.title: Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa
articles.body:
Trump Halts Army's Plans to Detonate Bomb-Making Chemicals In Iowa (arstechnica.com) 27
			
		 	
				President Trump has ordered the military to halt plans to detonate nearly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. "Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January," reports Ars Technica. From the report:  The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).
Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.
Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice's request to put a hold on the Army's permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

articles.title: CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal
articles.body:
CrowdStrike to Buy Zscaler In $44 Billion Deal 22
			
		 	
				CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire network security provider Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal. "The deal marks CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition to date and is among the largest in the sector as businesses consolidate and ramp up defenses to fend off AI-powered attacks," reports CNBC. The acquisition is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028. From the report:  "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely," CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said in a statement. "We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen."
CrowdStrike has been a major beneficiary of skyrocketing demand for AI security, with shares soaring about 80% this year as of Monday's open. Zscaler shares are up about 5% year to date after Monday's surge. Their combined market value exceeded $265 billion as of Friday's close, behind market leader Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.
[...] Analysts view the Zscaler deal as a major AI security opportunity, allowing CrowdStrike to capture more customer security spending and close a significant gap with Palo Alto. "The addition of ZS to CRWD's platform could bring more breadth in an era of vendor consolidation and, more importantly, network security to position the company more effectively for rising demand for AI Sovereignty," wrote analysts at JPMorgan.

articles.title: One Man's Quest to End Daylight Savings
articles.body:
At a rally in Mississippi not long ago, Donald Trump complained about the reason for his frequent tardiness. “I’m always late. You know, I had a big meeting and I was an hour late. I said, ‘How?’ ” he told the crowd. “Daylight-saving time. We change it twice a year. . . . It’s ridiculous.” Trump has been urging the Senate to approve the Sunshine Protection Act—which was passed by the House in July and would make daylight-saving time permanent—before the bill expires at the end of the current Congress, on January 3rd.
His speech recalled an episode of HBO’s “Veep” in which Congressman Jonah Ryan is two hours late to a meeting after adjusting his clock the wrong way. “That’s impossible,” Ryan says. “I set my watch back for daylight-savings time. I springed backwards!” Told that he should have sprung forward, he’s irate: “Have you ever watched girls’ gymnastics? That makes no sense!”
“It’s a naturally funny topic,” Scott Yates said late last month, the day before the clocks were set back. Yates, a sixty-one-year-old former journalist, has spent a decade trying to end the changing of the clocks. “Some people plan their vacations around golf,” he said. “I use frequent-flier miles to fly to Michigan to testify.”
He was sitting outside a former chapel in Liberia, Costa Rica, to which he relocated from Colorado, in 2024. The country does not change the clocks. “It’s not the No. 1 reason I moved here, but it’s on the list,” he said. He wore Birkenstocks and no watch. Yates began his crusade after he read the book “A Complaint Free World.” “The idea is, if you can’t do something about it, you shouldn’t complain about it,” he said. “Robbing an hour of sleep just always annoyed me.” So he started a blog (locktheclock.net) in which he compiles research on the topic.
Yates found that studies linked the “spring forward” clock change—where people lose an hour of sleep—to a rise in heart attacks and medical incidents involving human error, while the “fall backward” clock change—where it gets dark earlier—led to an increase in fatal auto accidents. Both changes are associated with a spike in strokes.
Within a couple of years, legislators in more than a dozen states started contacting Yates about his writing. He’s helped draft bills, spoken at hearings, and, last year, testified before the Senate Commerce Committee, advocating to end clock changing. (His proposal would give states two years to decide which time to lock in.) He concluded his testimony with a story about how scientists often avoid changing lab rats’ schedules after a clock change because it disrupts results. “At long last, can we treat our citizens with the decency that we treat our lab rats?” he asked the senators.
Yates often gets e-mails from people with their own ideas about how to solve the problem. Computer programmers reach out suggesting that we stop using time zones and time changes altogether and put the whole world on Coördinated Universal Time, the international time standard. In New York, this might mean waking up at noon and having lunch at 6 P.M. “It’s never going to happen,” Yates said.
The idea of daylight-saving time was first implemented in Germany during the First World War, to save on energy costs, but it had built steam earlier in Europe as a health movement and was helped along by a golf-loving Englishman named William Willett, who liked to go riding early in the morning. “He was me a hundred years earlier,” Yates said. In 1907, Willett distributed a pamphlet called “The Waste of Daylight,” promoting a plan for four twenty-minute advances in the clock throughout the year. It went nowhere.
Around the same time, the National Baseball League wanted more light for evening games, while movie-theatre executives wanted less, thinking that darkness might drive people into cinemas. In the states, daylight-saving time was implemented as a fragmented system throughout the World Wars and assorted energy crises. In New York City, in 1951, Grand Central Terminal was home to two railroads that used different times. In the early sixties, there were twenty-three different combinations of start and end dates for daylight-saving time in Iowa alone. The Times described it as “time schizophrenia.” To remedy the clock anarchy, the Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the dates for daylight-saving time and gave states the option of moving to permanent Standard Time. Only Hawaii, Arizona (except the Navajo Nation), Puerto Rico, and a few other U.S. territories do not change the clocks.
“Time doesn’t exist,” Yates said. “The thing that we call time is just what we all agree on.” The Sunshine Protection Act is the closest he has come to getting his way, but the House bill is slightly different than what he advocated for. “Washington is just so dysfunctional,” he said. “If this was a thing with money behind it, it would’ve been worked out.” He added, “I’m so worried about Trump being in favor of it, because I don’t want to ruin it for another fifty years.” ♦

Yates found that studies linked the “spring forward” clock change—where people lose an hour of sleep—to a rise in heart attacks and medical incidents involving human error, while the “fall backward” clock change—where it gets dark earlier—led to an increase in fatal auto accidents. Both changes are associated with a spike in strokes.
Within a couple of years, legislators in more than a dozen states started contacting Yates about his writing. He’s helped draft bills, spoken at hearings, and, last year, testified before the Senate Commerce Committee, advocating to end clock changing. (His proposal would give states two years to decide which time to lock in.) He concluded his testimony with a story about how scientists often avoid changing lab rats’ schedules after a clock change because it disrupts results. “At long last, can we treat our citizens with the decency that we treat our lab rats?” he asked the senators.
Yates often gets e-mails from people with their own ideas about how to solve the problem. Computer programmers reach out suggesting that we stop using time zones and time changes altogether and put the whole world on Coördinated Universal Time, the international time standard. In New York, this might mean waking up at noon and having lunch at 6 P.M. “It’s never going to happen,” Yates said.
The idea of daylight-saving time was first implemented in Germany during the First World War, to save on energy costs, but it had built steam earlier in Europe as a health movement and was helped along by a golf-loving Englishman named William Willett, who liked to go riding early in the morning. “He was me a hundred years earlier,” Yates said. In 1907, Willett distributed a pamphlet called “The Waste of Daylight,” promoting a plan for four twenty-minute advances in the clock throughout the year. It went nowhere.
Around the same time, the National Baseball League wanted more light for evening games, while movie-theatre executives wanted less, thinking that darkness might drive people into cinemas. In the states, daylight-saving time was implemented as a fragmented system throughout the World Wars and assorted energy crises. In New York City, in 1951, Grand Central Terminal was home to two railroads that used different times. In the early sixties, there were twenty-three different combinations of start and end dates for daylight-saving time in Iowa alone. The Times described it as “time schizophrenia.” To remedy the clock anarchy, the Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the dates for daylight-saving time and gave states the option of moving to permanent Standard Time. Only Hawaii, Arizona (except the Navajo Nation), Puerto Rico, and a few other U.S. territories do not change the clocks.
“Time doesn’t exist,” Yates said. “The thing that we call time is just what we all agree on.” The Sunshine Protection Act is the closest he has come to getting his way, but the House bill is slightly different than what he advocated for. “Washington is just so dysfunctional,” he said. “If this was a thing with money behind it, it would’ve been worked out.” He added, “I’m so worried about Trump being in favor of it, because I don’t want to ruin it for another fifty years.” ♦

articles.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
articles.body:
In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”
Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”
The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.
xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.
Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.
The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors:
“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

articles.body:

articles.title: Levent Alpöge comments on his Riemann Hypothesis proof
articles.body:
Stupid things I did:
1. 250,000+ pages was a joke guys!, I find big number extremely hilarious. I tried to make it clear by the level of pedantry of the reals total ordered statement in the main theorem, but people ran with it unfortunately and I didn’t feel like talking on social media in the days after the announcement, though I did have a good time with the memes. Sorry!!! (Similarly with our YM4 existence I found it extremely funny that we were slowly working through 60,000 pages of slop, though the committee asking for Lean made me feel dumb about wasting our time with that. But 60,000 funny.) Tao advises to not joke in papers, see also the Big Lebowski reference I shoehorned, I now understand why… I didn’t feel comfortable having any slop writeup attached to this problem, and I figured I can’t produce anything readable anyway, so I went off the Lean to lengthmaxx.
2. The Lean is full of garbage obviously, but compiles, but all criticism of such garbage is totally reasonable and accepted, I should have cleaned it up but it was randomly difficult to for various strange reasons. Mea culpa…
3. @scottnarmstrong clocked me, indeed even as a student there were theorems that took me the better part of a decade to write up, but with this one I should hopefully be more responsible. (I really was yoloing a lot in there, I bet most is unnecessary in the end, admittedly the lazy thing to do would be to wait because it’ll simplify massively…)
4. I forgot to emphasize what I think is the point. Arguments like these, cool, but they are the raw inputs when interpolating definitions. We don’t have the / an “H^1 object” over number fields, and probably for a layperson the fact that we fight hard for these arguments for the purpose of definitions is not clear a priori (that’s at least my philosophy). Just like I knew I must fight for an utterly simple Weil / Deligne, I feel Riemann should be easy, and any real difficulty is an indication our setup is just dumb at the moment.
