articles.title: Shirudo: OpenAI and Cisco's open-source runtime for shielding unpatched Linux
articles.body:
OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo
An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts
OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test(opens in a new window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.
We’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.
Testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.
Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.
Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.
OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:
- Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.
- Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.
- Trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.
- Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.
The Shirudo technical walkthrough(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here(opens in a new window).
Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.
Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to quickly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.
We will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.
OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo(opens in a new window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.
Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.
- Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart(opens in a new window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.
- Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab(opens in a new window).
- Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar(opens in a new window).
We’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, new shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub(opens in a new window), read the docs(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website.
The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy.
The Senate Banking Committee has jurisdiction over export control policies that are designed to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies, such as chips capable of powering AI models, from falling into the hands of foreign governments and militaries.
The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations.
It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Accuses Google of Kneecapping Its Android Partners Using Pixel Exclusives
articles.body:
GrapheneOS Accuses Google of Kneecapping Its Android Partners Using Pixel Exclusives (itsfoss.com) 26
			
		 	
				Last year Slashed reported that the privacy- and security-focused Android fork GrapheneOS was "partnering with a major Android OEM to bring its hardened, de-Googled OS to Snapdragon-powered flagship phones." 
And early this November Motorola announced their upcoming high end Signature 27 phone would include official support for GrapheneOS as an OS option, the first Motorola device supporting GrapheneOS.
But the nonprofit GrapheneOS project has a new problem, reports the blog It's FOSS :
GrapheneOS has accused Google of leaning on phone makers to keep away from the project. The claim came in a thread on X [Thursday], where the project says makers were questioned about working with it, then threatened over their Google app licensing.... The project says Google is working against GrapheneOS itself and expects it to go further. It sees Pixel bootloaders being locked down eventually and Play Integrity, an API it calls illegal, being pushed harder. And if that were to happen, Android forks would struggle to survive under that.  
GrapheneOS believes some of Google's conduct breaks US criminal law and that antitrust violations can put individuals in prison. It wants to talk to the [U.S.] Department of Justice and says earlier cases against Google left its most serious violations largely untouched. Supporters are being asked for introductions to prosecutors and regulators, with assurances that the project has the necessary resources to carry on no matter what happens.  
GrapheneOS says more Android features and updates now stay Pixel only, leaving other hardware partners behind.

articles.title: GTA VI’s pretentious puzzler makes indie developers feel ‘part of larger culture’
articles.body:
One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.
GTA VI’s pretentious puzzler makes indie developers feel ‘part of larger culture’
Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and big-budget blockbusters.
Developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV shows you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.
“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.)
But Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang said, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it launched in 2012.
“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”
Rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.)
Barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”
Yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang said. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”

articles.title: Amazon is taking orders for the Moto Tag 3 before it’s even been announced
articles.body:
Motorola’s unannounced Moto Tag 3 has been listed for sale online, just five months after the Moto Tag 2 went on sale in the US, and before any official announcement of a follow-up. The listing on Amazon UK was spotted by X user @matteventu, and shows the tracker in a “Pantone Lucent White” color option, with a price of £24.96 (about $33) and a 1-4 month shipping estimate.
Amazon is taking orders for the Moto Tag 3 before it’s even been announced
The Amazon UK listing for Motorola’s new tracking tag has been live since Friday.
A second image shared by leaker Evan Blass also shows a vibrant purple version of the new tracking tag, which is described as “Pantone Indigo Blue” on a separate Amazon Italy listing. Both are new color options, with the Moto Tag 2 only currently available in orange or a grey-ish beige. While the Moto Tag 3 name suggests this is a follow-up to the Moto Tag 2, there don’t appear to be any major hardware differences between the two trackers.
Both use a replaceable CR2032 battery, claim to provide more than 500 days of battery life, and support UWB in Android Find Hub, among other similarities. The XT2561-1 model number seen on the back of the Moto Tag 3 images also matches that of the Moto Tag 2. That could mean that the Moto Tag 3 name is an error and these are just new color options for the Tag 2.
We’ve asked Motorola for clarification and will update if we hear back.

articles.title: Freeing the iPod Nano 5G
articles.body:
A few years ago, CUB3D demonstrated unsigned code execution on the iPod nano 6G and 7G through ipod_sun, a font-based exploit. Whether the same approach would work on the 5G was still an open question.
I wanted to get Rockbox running on the nano 5G, so I set out to adapt the exploit. My motivation was simple: an up-to-date music player without an internet connection. I built a fully untethered boot chain that loads Rockbox from the nano 5G’s NAND, with no computer or button sequence needed after installation. I also found a way to make the existing exploit fully untethered on the nano 7G, and likely the 6G too.
Existing DFU exploits, including q3k’s wInd3x, provide code execution on the nano 5G, but booting custom code this way requires a computer each time. I used wInd3x to explore the device and develop a convenient, fully untethered exploit. The firmware details below refer to the latest nano 5G firmware, 1.0.2 (34A20020).
The catch with ipod_sun
The nano 5G’s NAND flash appears through a flash translation layer (FTL) as a logical disk with 4 KiB sectors. Its partition table separates a small private area for persistent device state, a firmware partition containing boot programs and resources, and a data volume for user files. The firmware partition has a directory of named images; the fonts live inside rsrc, a resource volume formatted as FAT16.
The original ipod_sun chain combines a resource-validation bypass with a font-parser vulnerability. Apple’s firmware directory identifies the normal operating system as osos, the disk-mode program as disk, and the resource image containing fonts as rsrc. The disk-mode boot path does not request the resource signature check used by normal OS boot.
Swapping the disk and osos directory entries exploits that difference: selecting disk mode now launches Apple’s regular OS under the disk-mode policy. The OS still reads its fonts, but the bootloader has not required a valid signature for the modified resource image.
The font then triggers CVE-2010-1797, the FreeType CFF stack-overflow vulnerability also known through the star exploit. A malformed font program corrupts the parser’s stack and redirects execution. My 5G port adapts that technique to the device’s font and execution context.
The swapped images remain on disk, but each restart still requires choosing disk mode with the device’s buttons. A normal boot selects the other entry. I wanted a better experience, with the modified font loading through the normal OS path.
Finding a bypass in the normal boot path
The bootloader is organized into EFI-style modules stored as Portable Executable (PE) images. The module that passes execution to the next boot stage decides whether to validate rsrc. It first asks the PrivateData module for FirmwareStatus, which comes from an authenticated record in the private NAND partition.
The decisive branch is below. This is reconstructed C from the reverse-engineered routine, with unrelated fuse handling and protocol setup omitted.
A value of 2 returns success before the resource-validation query. Bit 0 must remain clear: it is checked first, so 3 would reject the boot attempt. Tracing the restore OS shows that it sets the status to 1 during firmware transfer and clears it to 0 at the end. This suggests an update-in-progress guard that prevents booting an incomplete installation.
Apple’s resource-mount path writes status 2 only on the first successful boot, after rsrc has passed signature verification. My hypothesis is that this avoids repeating signature verification to shorten boot time or reduce energy use.
This is the second bypass. Instead of disguising the normal OS as disk mode, I can leave the firmware directory alone and supply a valid private record with bit 1 set. The normal boot path then accepts the modified resource image, and its font delivers code execution automatically.
The record lives in the private partition, identified by MBR type 0x3e. On the 5G layout I examined, the partition begins at logical block 1, with 4 KiB blocks. The bootloader reads a 512-byte header from its start. The status-bearing format begins with the little-endian magic PRVD and has this layout:
The integrity tag is device-specific, so creating and saving a valid PRVD record requires code execution on that iPod.
The tag is the first 16 bytes of the SHA-1 digest, encrypted with the device’s hardware AES UID key, selected through key slot 2. It authenticates the private header, but as the authentication is constructed on device we can falsify it if we have code execution.
Using emCORE to make it persistent
To inspect and update the private partition, I adapted emCORE, an older framework from freemyipod’s earlier iPod exploitation and boot work. It provided an existing USB-controlled environment to extend for the 5G.
I wrote the nano 5G NAND driver and integrated it into emCORE alongside the flash translation layer (FTL) and hardware AES access. I’ll cover the flash memory sequencer subsystem (FMSS), which enables NAND writes, in a future post. The FTL presents logical sectors over physical flash; it is the layer through which I read and write the private record and install the modified font.
The private-status tool verifies the existing header and tag, constructs the updated record, and obtains its new tag from the device. It rechecks the partition table and header before writing, then flushes the write and reads it back. The tool writes a complete 4 KiB logical sector even though the bootloader only consumes the smaller header. This works on nano 5G hardware.
Once the private record and modified font are installed, they remain in NAND across restarts. emCORE and the host computer are needed for the installation workflow, not for each subsequent boot.
A bootloader in less than 28 KB
Reaching the font parser automatically solved persistence. The next constraint was fitting something useful inside the font. I wanted it to load Rockbox from storage, so the payload needed a NAND driver, a flash translation layer, a filesystem reader, and enough startup code to hand off reliably.
To fit, I compiled with size and link-time optimizations and had the linker remove unused sections. The Rockbox kernel is stored on the device’s FAT32 partition and can be easily updated.
Taking control from the font parser
Code execution initially arrives in a damaged FreeType call frame. The stack has been corrupted, and Apple’s OS has left interrupts, DMA controllers, timers, caches, and address translation configured for its own use. Jumping straight into a large C program would carry that state into storage initialization.
I split the bootstrap into two images. The first is the 808-byte assembly stub at 0x22050000. Its job is to leave the parser context: mask IRQs and FIQs, switch to a private stack, stop inherited timer activity, quiesce DMA and clock domains, and clean up caches and the MMU before entering the main payload. It replaces the damaged stack and then jumps to the Rockbox kernel loader.
The second image is the main loader at 0x22060000. Its entry code disables the watchdog before starting the NAND scan, installs its own stack, and clears the uninitialized-data area before calling C. The watchdog matters because reconstructing the logical flash mapping can take several seconds; a reset in the middle would stop the boot before it ever found Rockbox.
This separation keeps the most fragile stage small. The assembly stub establishes a controlled execution environment; the main payload can then do the more substantial storage work in freestanding C.
Reading NAND and starting Rockbox
At the hardware level, the NAND driver uses FMSS, a programmable microcontroller, to communicate with the NAND chips. lemonjesus’s earlier work on the S5L8702 sequencer, published as S5L8702-FMISS-Tools, documents its instruction set and provides tools for inspecting and building bytecode. That research is important prior work for understanding this part of the storage hardware; my work here uses the sequencer to read NAND as part of the nano 5G boot path.
The loader first checks that the microsecond timer used for driver timeouts is running. It then initializes the read-only NAND and FTL stack, mounts the FAT filesystem, and opens /.rockbox/rockbox.ipod. The core sequence follows the Rockbox bootloader’s own file-loading path:
The file loader checks the Rockbox model identifier and checksum, then leaves the executable image at 0x08000000. The final handoff keeps interrupts masked, cleans and invalidates caches, drains pending writes, and branches to that address. Rockbox’s startup code takes over from there. If storage, mounting, or image loading fails, the payload shows the failing stage on the LCD and stops.
Result and limits
On my nano 5G, the result is a cold, battery-powered boot straight into Rockbox, with no USB connection and no disk-mode button sequence. The PRVD partition setting skips rsrc validation and, when combined with the star exploit, enables untethered boot straight into Rockbox. The main constraint is that the font payload is limited to 27,874 bytes. Installation and restoration procedures, along with the reverse-engineering notes and build details, are in the nano5g_bootstub and nano5g_emCORE repositories below.
I have confirmed that the private-data partition works the same way on the nano 7G, which suggests the method will likely work on the 6G too. I plan to get the nano 4G and 5G Rockbox ports into good shape before applying this method to the 6G and 7G.
References
- nano5g_bootstub: the font exploit, PRVD analysis, two-stage Rockbox loader, and exact size budget.
- nano5g_emCORE: the emCORE port, NAND read/write tools, authenticated private-record updates, and installation procedure.
- CUB3D’s ipod_sun: the earlier nano 6G/7G chain combining the disk-mode swap with a modified font.
- q3k, “wInd3x, the iPod Bootrom exploit 10 years too late”: the USB/DFU entry point used to run unsigned code during setup, with background on the iPod boot chain.
- Apple’s firmware update catalog: lists nano 5G firmware 1.0.2 (34A20020) under iPod software family 34.
- CVE-2010-1797: the existing FreeType CFF vulnerability used by the font exploit.
- freemyipod’s emCORE source: the original framework and earlier device targets on which the nano 5G adaptation builds.
- lemonjesus’s S5L8702-FMISS-Tools: earlier reverse engineering of the flash-controller sequencer, with instruction-set documentation and bytecode tools.
- n3g_fmss: my documentation of the nano 3G flash memory sequencer.
- n4g_fmss: my documentation of the nano 4G flash memory sequencer.
- Rockbox source: upstream firmware, storage, filesystem, and image-loading code reused in this work.

articles.title: The Beauty of Artists' Studios
articles.body:
issue 21 November 2026
Sir Frederic Leighton was president of the Royal Academy, one of the foremost sculptors and painters of his day. And yet one imagines his neighbours may still have been taken aback when, in 1881, he added to his home, on a quiet street in Kensington, an Arab Hall three storeys tall, topped with a crescent moon.
At least they could finally see what the artist had been up to on his annual solo trips to the east: shopping. Inside, Moorish, Turkish, Byzantine and Pompeiian tiles and styles mingle like layers on a cake, and yet the effect is beautiful, perhaps because Leighton commissioned star ceramicists Walter Crane and William De Morgan to bring all his finds together. The centrepiece was a tinkling fountain and impluvium, complete with goldfish.
Today the fish are gone, but Leighton House is lovingly restored, and still a bold aesthetic gambit. Opulently fitted out with chartreuse silk walls and considered effects of light at every turn, it was Leighton’s mini-museum and his stage set, where visitors stepped into the atmosphere of his paintings. Built to Leighton’s specification by George Aitchison, it was designed for display and hospitality on the grandest scale – Queen Victoria visited in 1869. But Leighton’s bedroom, opposite his studio, was plain and monk-like, with a little single bed, as if he were married, in a sense, to art.
A new show, Magic and Mess: The Artist’s Studio Revealed, which will be in the exhibition space until March next year, puts Leighton House in context, with 56 paintings, drawings and albumen photographic prints depicting artists’ studios from the long 19th-century. Although Leighton House is the only purpose-built Victorian artist’s studio-home now open to the public in London, it was once of a type, comparable with the bohemian palaces of his peers, those of G.F. Watts, Val Prinsep, Marcus Stone and J. Pettie (whose home, The Lothians, on Fitzjohns Avenue was a bold Scottish baronial) – all now lost and fabled.
Studios ranged from high to low, ‘basilica to bedsit’, as the catalogue has it. Antonio Canova’s studio and birthplace in Rome formed part of a must-see visitors’ complex, including consecrated temple. But at the other extreme, Sir Joseph Nollekens’s studio in Fitzrovia was shabby and troubled by rats, and the local brothel-keeper and supplier of life models, Mrs Lobb, kept coming in demanding money. All this was exposed in a tell-all memoir by a former employee published in 1829.
Most of the works on display in Magic and Mess come from Katrin Bellinger, who collects on the theme of ‘the artist at work’. Bellinger, formerly a dealer at Colnaghi specialising in Old Master drawings, is a benefactor of the arts, with a penchant for art about art; paintings about painting.
I say penchant, but her collection, growing since 1985, now includes 2,000 pieces. They rotate between being stored at her research facility, going on loan, and hanging on the walls of her home, not far from Leighton House. Initially she specialised in works on paper, but when her family expressed a preference for living with daylight, she started broadening her acquisitions.
‘I am fascinated by the mystique of the creative process,’ she tells me. ‘Artists on the road, artists in the studio, artists’ models – there are so many avenues to explore. That’s why I never got bored. I love the stories, the connections and finding great work by more obscure artists.’ For example, the painting of Alma-Tadema’s first London home, Townshend House, by Emily Epps Williams, the artist’s sister-in-law. It is a lovely, detailed panel painting – long and thin (82cm x 19cm), like looking through a keyhole. A sinuous blue hookah pipe hose lies negligently across the threshold, implying that the decor itself – the secret gleams of old gold in the dark corners, the daylight intensifying the red frescoed ceiling to blood – is in an altered state.
But in 1880s, when she painted this panel, Townshend House was already a memory, badly damaged when a passing barge on Regent’s Canal exploded, carrying nuts, coffee, petroleum and gunpowder: you can imagine the mess. The Alma-Tademas moved to St John’s Wood and began decorating afresh, with zeal; Emily Epps Williams completed no other known subjects.
The signifiers for a 19th-century artist included, of course, the brushes, the beret and the flaçon of wine. But also, the artist’s stove. It was a practicality, especially if a model was going to undress – and a symbol of passion and the creative spark. Once you get your eye in, you notice them in so many depictions of artists. Cézanne’s soot-black pot-boiler, grumpy, dumpy, but tenaciously alight, is on display, loaned from the National Gallery – an early work from about 1865, which he gave to Émile Zola, his childhood friend.
Successful artists’ studios were bedecked with objets: bronze jugs, feathers, rich fabrics, rugs, palms, taxidermy. There would be assorted hands, arms and casts. By the 1880s this was known as ‘Makartstil’ after the lavish interior of Hans Makart’s studio in Vienna. Leighton, though more restrained, still had a peacock (stuffed). Even the unsuccessful artist, the bohemian wannabe, had to have some objets, as we see in the satirical staged photograph ‘Glory and the Stew’ (Marie-Alexandre Alophe, 1858). Here, turning in one easy gesture from his easel to his lunch, the humble artist nevertheless has two useful treasures, hanging on the stovepipe behind him: two plaster-cast ears.
If windows were an obsession for artists, so, too, were window shades, seen here in opulent Mexican onyx (Alma-Tadema’s ‘In My Studio’, 1893) or Moorish tracery (Théodor Jacques Ralli, photographed in his Paris studio by Edmond Bénard, 1882). In ‘The Studio’, from c.1910, Sir William Orpen uses terrible light from badly controlled Venetian blinds to create a bold painterly pattern. But almost a century earlier, in Kalman Dery’s ‘The Painter’s Studio’ (1883), the struggling artist cannot yet see how to make everyday experience into art, and lies there, becalmed, with a drab improvised sheet over the window, plus some desiccated corn stalks representing, perhaps, his dried-up inspiration.
Artists’ paraphernalia range from the set squares and mahlstick that project such a calm air of mastery in ‘Caspar David Friedrich in his Studio’ (1811) by Georg Kersting, to the teetering piles of picture references and scattered pencils that surround Victor-Charles-François Mongodin’s ‘A Painter’ (1850). The last seems like chaos, but look closer and the artist is clearly in the ultimate flow state, the mountain range of mess his perfect working conditions.
‘When painters depict painters, they often bring their best game,’ says Bellinger. ‘My parents collected expressionists because that was what you collected in Germany after the war, because the Old Masters were tainted by the Third Reich.’ She went to art school but ‘thankfully stopped after that, as I had no talent. I love to see artists at work. I enjoy the sense of peering over their shoulder, seeing how they do it.’
The artists here are often wearing slippers, hunched over, their intense concentration amplified, twinned with that of the unseen artist who is painting them. But the albumen silver photographic prints on display in the final room of this exhibition show no such intimacy, with the master artists rarely depicted at work, but posing for the camera, like Lord Leighton, dressed smartly, and performatively holding his brushes and palette.
Leighton was fastidiously respectable – the first artist to join the peerage by dint of his talent – and his models had their own off-street entrance and staircase up to his studio, with a changing area and fireplace. It was a practical working studio: the ‘picture slot’ in the wall meant his largest canvases could be posted out and winched down to the pavement without having to be removed from their stretchers. The same space became an otherworldly concert hall at night, when Bach’s Chaconne was played under the gold-painted dome in the presence of the artist and his paintings.
But the maximalist, objet-stuffed studio was not to last, as we see from Matisse’s ‘Studio Under the Eaves’ (on loan from the Fitzwilliam Museum). Painted in 1903, the darkness of the empty attic implies that all the artist needs is the life-giving sunlight from the window, its ceaselessly fascinating reflections and shadows, and one flower. Fauvism and freedom are coming! The artist, as this absorbing exhibition reveals, often provides the most incisive commentary on art.
Magic and Mess: The Artist’s Studio Revealed is at Leighton House until 21 March 2027.

articles.title: VP ≠ VNP over Every Field
articles.body:
For every field, circuits for the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, and for the permanent outside characteristic 2, need more than m^(c (log m)^(1/3)) gates for all large m. The same holds for approximating circuits. So VP is a proper subset of VNP, and VNP is not contained in the closure of VP. This does not settle P vs NP.
The result was discovered by an internal research Claude model. This folder holds the paper and its Lean 4 formalization. Both were written by AI models, and no human mathematician has checked the proof.
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
paper.pdf: VP ≠ VNP over every field, by Claude (Anthropic). The full proof is its appendix.
1. Read the statement. Statement.lean states all of the above and imports only Mathlib. Lean checks the proofs, but no machine checks that this file says what is claimed. Appendix Q of paper.pdf lists the Lean counterparts of the numbered statements (Table 3) and says where they differ.
2. Check the proofs. With elan installed, in this folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
The build prints sorry warnings from Challenge.lean only, which states the theorems without proofs for the fuller check. The last command should name no axiom other than propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The fuller check is the one this repository's CI runs, bash ../.github/scripts/comparator-check.sh (Linux): Comparator compares the statements with Challenge.lean and re-checks the proofs with a second, independently written kernel, nanoda.

articles.title: Next gaming monitor should still be an OLED
articles.body:
They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED
Go for the burn
Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.
Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.
The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.
We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.
That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.
The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.
Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.
With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.
While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.
I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.
The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.
Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.
For what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.
After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.
All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.
If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.
So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.
Indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.
Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.
Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.
However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.
In both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.
Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.
When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.
If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.
Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).
Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.
The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.
Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.
Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.
Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

articles.title: How should an LLM see a computer?
articles.body:
Introduction
Claude Code and Codex can both use your computer. Under the hood they work in a similar manner: both can give the model a screenshot and an accessibility tree, a text description of every button on screen, and let it click by position or by naming an element.
The text version of the screen was built decades ago, for people who couldn’t see it. In 1984, two IBM mathematicians, Jim Thatcher and his former thesis adviser, Jesse Wright, who was blind, started a side project to read the PC’s screen out loud. When GUIs turned the screen into pixels, apps had to start describing themselves instead. Microsoft shipped Active Accessibility in 1997, Sun started AT-SPI for Linux in 2001, and Apple added its Accessibility API in 2002.
This text has been useful for agents too. On the 2024 OSWorld benchmark, models looking only at screenshots completed about one task in twenty, whereas most models reading the screen as text performed better.
How do those results hold up with stronger models? We tested screenshots on their own and with the accessibility tree on seven models, and used the results to decide how our QA agent, TREX, should see the screen.
What's so hard about clicking a button?
A person clicks a button by moving the mouse to it. A model, on the other hand, looks at a screenshot and has to write the coordinates out as text (e.g., ‘x=523, y=217’) before clicking on it. Getting these numbers off by a few pixels can mean it clicks the wrong thing.
The same button sits at different coordinates on different screen and window sizes, so the guesses get worse when the resolution changes.
Also, the model’s vision works against it as it doesn’t see a screenshot pixel by pixel. The image is initially shrunk to fit the model's size limit, then cut into tiny squares, each dozens of pixels wide. But a click still has to land on one exact pixel.
Small targets are hard. On ScreenSpot-Pro, a 2025 benchmark with tiny targets on high resolution screens, the best model at release hit the right target only 18.9% of the time. Anthropic’s own docs warn that Claude “might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates.”
When OSWorld came out in 2024, human testers were able to complete 72% of its tasks, and the best model about 12%. The authors found that models struggled with two things: turning ‘click Save’ into the right point on the screen, and knowing how to operate the software.
The first problem has a seemingly obvious fix. The accessibility tree already reveals each button's location, so the model doesn't have to go through the trouble of finding pixels. Go one step further, and the model doesn’t even need coordinates; it can pick a button by ID and let the harness click it. To test this, we built three setups, each building upon the last:
- Screenshots alone
- Adding an accessibility tree (clicking by coordinates)
- Adding clicks by element IDs
Every setup used the same agent on 172 OSWorld tasks, with one attempt per task, a 50-step limit and low reasoning effort, scored by OSWorld’s own graders.
Starting with screenshots
The model runs in a loop where it first sees a screenshot and past actions, picks an action (click coordinates, type or press keys), and then looks at the changes. It’s the simplest way to give a model a computer, and the one most agents start with. OSWorld’s baseline agent supports it, and Anthropic described its first computer use model as looking at screenshots and counting how many pixels to move the cursor.
We ran the same screenshot agent across seven OpenAI models:
On our 172 tasks, GPT-4.1 scored a mere 5.4% with screenshots alone, while the more recent GPT-6.1 Sol scored 83.8%. On the much harder OSWorld 2.0 offline set, OpenAI reports a score of 71.4% for GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. The gap between the two models raised questions: do stronger models even need the tree, and can it help weaker ones catch up?
Adding the accessibility tree
Here, the model sees the screenshot with an accessibility tree beside it. We were interested in the tree because it can just tell the model what’s there, like a button labeled “Save” and where it sits. The model still clicks by coordinates here. The tree lists each element's position and dimensions in pixels, so the model can work out where to click after doing the math. With the clicking kept constant, the only thing that changed was what the model saw.
OSWorld runs on Linux, and so our agents read AT-SPI. The app's toolkit, such as GTK and Qt, describes what's on screen and passes on those descriptions to any program that asks for them, without prompting the user for permissions. Also, while testing, we realized that GIMP was missing from the tree until we added back an environment variable set at login.
In the evals, trees helped every model that struggled with screenshots. GPT-5.2 went from 15.8% with screenshots alone to 36.2% after the tree was added, and GPT-4.1 from 5.4% to 20.6%. On the other hand, stronger models barely moved. GPT-6.1 Sol got 82.7% when the tree was added, slightly lower than with screenshots alone (83.8%) and none of the three strongest models changed by a statistically significant amount.
Clicking by ID
Next, we gave each element in the tree an ID. The model can simply name the element it wants and the harness clicks it. This bypasses the problem of clicking the exact pixel.
For weaker models, ID clicks boosted performance on top of the tree. GPT-5.2 went from 36.2% with the tree + coordinates to 52.8% when it clicked by ID, and GPT-4.1 from 20.6% to 29.3%. Put together, the tree and ID clicks more than tripled GPT-5.2’s score with screenshots alone (15.8%).
Again, this experiment didn't do much for the strongest models. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 82.7% clicking by coordinates and 82.1% clicking by ID.
It depends on the model
For the three strongest models, neither step made a difference. Across both steps, the four weaker models gained 9 to 37 points with the tree and ID clicks, more than doubling their scores in three of four cases. If you’re building on weaker models, the tree is still worth adding.
Some apps publish no tree at all. A canvas app like Figma publishes its toolbar buttons, but the canvas itself is just pixels, and a game like Doom is pixels from top to bottom. Even in apps with a good tree, some bugs only show on screen, like text that overflows its box. The screenshot covers all of these.
TREX Computer Use
Code review catches bugs in the diff. Some bugs only exist when the software is running: a button that can’t be clicked, a label that runs off the edge of the window. Until now, catching those took a person opening the app and simulating the user flow. By writing more code and touching more of the UI than any team can check by hand, coding agents have made it hard for programmers to keep up.
That’s why we built computer use into TREX. It runs the changes in your pull request on an actual desktop and uses the app the way a person would, so you can see that the feature you asked for is the one that got built.
How TREX sees the screen came out of these experiments. It runs on the best models and relies on the screenshot at every step. It uses the accessibility tree to click by ID when it can, and coordinates when the tree doesn't have the element, like a canvas or a game.
How a model should see the screen depends on the model, so we'll rerun these experiments each time a new one comes out and update TREX when the answer changes.
When something breaks on screen, TREX catches it, and shows you what happened.
Try TREX on your next pull request.

articles.title: Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo
articles.body:
00 Why?
I always come back to the Super Nintendo (SNES). It was my first console and it’s still my most potent source of nostalgia. It inspired my early interest in electronics as a teenager, designing circuits for mods and flash carts that I hoped to build one day. I followed the launch of Hackaday, Adafruit, and the progress of bunnie Huang’s Chumby and knew exactly what I wanted to do.
I dropped out of my final years of high school to study hands-on electronics at college, and continued on to university. Then, finally equipped with those skills I’d aspired to, I went off-track and spent the next fifteen years working in data, ML and software. A lot has changed in that time but I’m back now, picking up exactly where I left off.
The Super Network Adapter is an exercise in ‘16-bit futurism’, it aims to be a faithful peripheral to the original SNES hardware and what we imagined the future might be back then: a wireless link to the net, sync’ing saves across devices and an uplink to AI.
01 Prototyping
The SNES never had a dedicated network port. The closest it came was the Satellaview, a modem peripheral connected to a hidden expansion port that could receive game broadcasts via satellite. There was also the XBAND, a modem that plugged into the cartridge slot and supported pass-through patching of specific games for online play. Reproducing the hardware of either of these today would be challenging, however most peripherals for the SNES took a much simpler route, they used one of the controller ports.
Controller Serial Link
      The SNES controller ports are small synchronous serial buses that a game can control, setting and reading individual lines and driving the clock. These ports have seven lines but in a typical controller cable, only five tend to be present, with the wires for D1 and IOBit left out. To make sourcing parts for this project easier, my design also only relies on the remaining five wires.
      
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
 │ ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────╮ │
 │ │  ●       ●       ●       ●   │  │   ●       ●       ●   │ │
 │ └──────────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────╯ │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
      1       2       3       4          5       6       7
      5v     CLK    Latch     D0         D1    IOBit    GND
    
    First I needed a protocol for talking over this serial link, which I iterated with Mesen and a virtual network adapter written in Lua simulating the controller port link. This protocol has the SNES writing to the Latch line and reading from the adapter on D0, one bit at a time (‘bit-banging’). Even with some optimisation (unrolling loops and ignoring mid-stream replies) this approach tops out at about 30 KB/s, but that’s enough for the ’90s.
    
Breadboard Version
The first physical prototype was built using a Pico 2 W dev board. The additional circuitry needed was very simple, just some pull-up resistors for CLK and Latch. The board’s RP2350A can handle the console’s 5v logic on its pins directly, and it has two cores: one can maintain the console link, while the other maintains the Wi-Fi network link, without juggling interrupts.
Controller port pinout
The prototype runs from USB, with the console’s 5v only feeding the pull-ups. I did not connect the SNES 5v to the Pico’s VBUS or VSYS while USB is plugged in. The Pico was powered on before the console so the RP2350’s pins were ready to handle 5v. The PCB design later can run on either supply.
02 Save sync
Adding Cloud Save or ‘Save Sync’ seemed the most practical use for a Wi-Fi connection. I often go back to the SNES and start a new game, but if I could continue playing that save file in RetroArch on my phone and then back to the SNES, it would fit into my life much more easily.
      Game save data is stored in battery-backed SRAM and in order for a game to send that through my adapter, I needed some of my own code to run. I already have a programmable flash cart for the SNES, so I wrote a utility to patch ROMs and inject this ‘save sync’ code into the reset vector. At power-on and whenever the console is reset, it syncs the save data through the adapter to a WebDAV server as saves/<core>/<name>.srm (the same path RetroArch uses) so the console save can be continued on the phone, and vice versa.
    
Joining Wi-Fi
First though, the adapter needs to join the local Wi-Fi network. I wanted an era-appropriate UI that can be run from a setup ROM (fig.2), which has you pick a network and type its password with an on-screen keyboard, one letter at a time. That felt most ‘authentic’ but I also made a second iteration that shows the typical QR code on the TV for setup via mobile phone.
The second version has the adapter set up a temporary network. Scanning the QR code with a phone joins the network and it then does the usual captive portal flow to open the adapter’s setup page, where the network and WebDAV auth details can be input in a much more user-friendly way.
Pushing and Pulling Saves
An important detail to get right was checking whether the save on the cartridge was newest, or whether to download a newer one from WebDAV. RetroArch keeps a manifest file with a hash of every save, so the adapter updates that too, comparing hashes to decide whether the cartridge or the server has the newest save. If both sides have changed, nothing is overwritten and the cartridge’s save goes to a conflicts folder to play it safe.
SRAM saves are small but this sync still has to run whenever a game starts, potentially introducing a delay. To avoid this, the save is split into chunks that each have their own checksum, so only the chunks that have changed are sent over the controller port. In practice this makes the save sync delay imperceptible, and only when an existing save is pulled by the SNES for the first time is there a 1-2s load screen.
03 AI dialogue
Naturally in 2026, an internet connection also means a connection to LLMs. The dialogue in SNES-era games tends to be fixed and unresponsive. In A Link to the Past, the villagers don’t react when you smash their pots (unlike in subsequent Zelda games). With the network adapter though, we can hook the game’s dialogue text renderer to swap out the original text for an in-character line generated by an LLM.
In order to prompt for dialogue, the LLM needs to be passed the game context, such as the character being interacted with and recent events. Since Link to the Past has been fully disassembled, it was possible to patch it to accumulate this state in RAM and push it out over the controller serial to the adapter and on to an LLM (via a proxy I ran on a local machine that holds the API key).
I tried a few different models and settled on Claude Opus 5.5, as cheaper models would break character or leak spoilers despite being prompted not to. I used LLM as a Judge evals to measure the proportion of responses that fit the context - Haiku scored 66%, Sonnet 90% and Opus 98%. The challenge was the time to first token of the LLM, for Haiku it was about 0.8 s but for Opus it averaged 2.2 s.
To avoid game-breaking delays from the LLM response times, I switched to speculatively generating the dialogue when Link approaches an NPC, storing the responses in a cache and invalidating them as the context updates. The delay from using a larger model was hidden and most NPC interactions had the response ready. This is a great way to burn tokens so probably not something to do for the full game duration!
04 Hardware
When designing the PCB version of the adapter (fig.0) I replicated the same architecture as the prototype, an RP2350A microcontroller that handles the 5v lines and maintains the serial link, with an ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi coprocessor that handles the Wi-Fi connection. These communicate with each other over UART, allowing each link to be maintained by a dedicated core.
┌─────────┐ port 2 ┌─────────┐ uart ┌──────────┐ wi-fi ┌────────┐
│ SNES    │──────▸ │ RP2350A │────▸ │ ESP32-C3 │~~~~~▸ │ cloud  │
│ 65816   │◂────── │ PIO     │◂──── │ TCP/TLS  │◂~~~~~ │ WebDAV │
└─────────┘        └─────────┘      └──────────┘       └────────┘
  3.58 MHz           150 MHz          160 MHz
      A PIO state machine on the RP2350 watches clock and latch, queueing the data and filtering out glitches shorter than 100 ns. This frees up the cores to prepare data to be sent over D0 while also talking to the C3.
    
The USB socket was included not just for flashing the board but also to support debugging it while it is powered from the SNES. This means the board needs to safely support taking a 5v supply from either the controller port or USB, and avoid backfeeding if both are connected. This is done with a LM66200 dual ideal diode. Supply can be taken from either source and we avoid the voltage drop that would come with using actual diodes. I’d seen some brownouts in tests on the breadboard, so designed the PCB with plenty of headroom for the LDO regulator even if the supply rail sags on a Wi-Fi burst.
While prototyping I also had issues when using series resistors on the link lines. This may be related to erratum RP2350-E9 in the A2 revision (stepping) of the RP2350A on my Pico 2 W. In the assembled PCB order I switched these to 0 Ω links, as they’re just for protection and I wasn’t sure which stepping the PCB would be assembled with. The boards turned out to have the fixed A4 stepping, so real resistors can go in next time.
05 Enclosure
The case is just a tray and a lid that sandwich the PCB, though I did want it to nod toward an era-appropriate design language. It was generated in code (build123d) using the PCB’s STEP files from KiCad, so that the design could be tested within a single 3D model.
The two halves join around the cable and the USB socket, and there are M2 pillars that align with the drilled holes in the PCB to hold everything together.
Since the PCB has a status LED, this design has a light pipe that channels that light up to become the dot of the etched Wi-Fi icon. It’s not the prettiest of designs, but I thought that was cute.
I’ve ordered a batch of these enclosures to be 3D printed and will update with actual photos once they arrive and the adapter is fully assembled. I’m also considering how to fabricate a single assembly that can insert directly into the controller port. Reach out at [email protected] if you’re interested!
06 Build log
- 65816 toolchain, headless emulator tests
- Breadboard link to port 2 working
- First save uploaded from the console
- PCB designed and ordered from JLCPCB
- PCBs arrive and work perfectly!
- Ordered 3D printed enclosures
- Awaiting delivery of enclosures

articles.title: Win4wine – Run Windows Shell as the Linux Desktop on Wine
articles.body:
Linux のデスクトップを、Windows XP のシェルで。
日本語 · English
Important

Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェルとして動かすプロジェクトです。
タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。
Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。
XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル（Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（docs/reactos.md）。
Windows 7 の ISO があれば、Windows 7 のシェル（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（docs/windows7.md）。
- XP のシェル: Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。
- Linux アプリとの統合: Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。 Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。
- 通知領域: Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。 XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の状態）も 出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の状態から作ります（AshesTom さんのフォークの XP Explorer から）。 ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの画面で接続できます。メニューや画面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。
- XP Explorer からの追加: フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、画面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。
配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、画像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、
ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、
よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（prefix/extras.py）。
- キーボードの配列: 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（localectl）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→
「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、
X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（session/keyboard.py）。
- 日本語入力: fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全角/半角）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。
- 日本語版と英語版の XP: どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判断し、字体（英語版は Tahoma など）、 ロケール、ようこそ画面をその XP に合わせます（英語版では日本語入力は設定しません）。
- Windows のアプリ: WoW64 の Wine 11.0 で、32bit と 64bit のアプリが動きます。端末で wine setup.exe と打つと、
インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。
- XP のようこそ画面: LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ画面とログオフの画面を出せます（任意）。 シェルが起動するまでは XP と同じ大きな「ようこそ」の画面を出します。
- XP のキー操作: Windows キー、Ctrl+Esc、Win+R、Win+E が使えます。
- クイック起動: タスクバーの右クリック →「ツール バー」→「クイック起動」で出せます（XP と ReactOS。Windows 7 は実機と同じく 「新規ツール バー」でクイック起動のフォルダを選びます）。スタートメニューから Linux のアプリのショートカットも置けます。 「デスクトップの表示」も実機と同じく、もう一度押すと窓が元に戻ります。
- 画面の拡大（DPI）: XP と同じ「DPI 設定」で、文字や部品を大きくできます（96・120・144 など）。
- 落ちても戻れる: XP のシェルが繰り返し落ちると、Wine 標準の explorer と xterm に切り替わります。
- Wayland のセッション（任意・X11 のセッション以上に実験的）: X11 のウィンドウマネージャーの代わりに、パッチを当てた labwc で 動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。 Wayland のアプリにもシェルの枠が付きます。作ったばかりで、確かめた範囲は X11 のセッションより狭く、既知の制限もあります（docs/wayland.md）。 ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。
- ReactOS のシェル（任意）: XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。 XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。
- Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的）: Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。 Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。
- Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）をご自身で用意してください。
- 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。
git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~/win4wine
cd ~/win4wine
scripts/setup.sh --media /path/to/WindowsXPSP3.iso --greeter
- 再起動すると、XP のようこそ画面からそのまま XP のシェルに入ります。
XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。
scripts/setup.sh --shell reactos --lang ja   # 英語なら --lang en
ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。
scripts/setup.sh --shell win7 --media /path/to/Windows7SP1x64.iso
ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP のクラシックなど）と文字の大きさは、後から変えられます（見た目と文字の大きさを変える）。
Warning
- Windows XP（と Windows 7）の ISO はご自身で入手してください。 このリポジトリにも導入スクリプトにも、Microsoft のファイルを 取得する処理はありません。ISO と取り出したファイルの扱いは、Microsoft の使用許諾に従ってください。
- 利用は自己責任でお願いします。 データの損失や不具合について、作者は責任を負いません。
- Microsoft とも Wine プロジェクトとも関係のない、非公式のプロジェクトです。
- 確かめているのは日本語版と英語版の XP SP3（x86）だけです。ほかの言語の XP も英語版と同じ設定で入れるので動くかもしれませんが、
一切試していません（setup.sh は警告を出して続けます）。
LightDM ─ XP のようこそ画面 (greeter/)
   └─ XP Shell セッション (session/supervisor.py)
        ├─ Wine 11.0 + 151 本のパッチ (wine/patches/)
        │    └─ XP の explorer.exe, shell32.dll, …（ISO から取り出したもの。ReactOS や Windows 7 のシェルではそれらのもの）
        ├─ bridge-wm: X11 のウィンドウマネージャー + Win32 の代理ウィンドウ (bridge-wm/)
        │    （Wayland のセッションでは、ウィンドウマネージャーの代わりにパッチを当てた labwc。wayland/）
        └─ fcitx5 + Mozc, トレイの仲介 (bridge-wm/tray.py)
仕組みや設計の詳しい説明は docs/ にまとめています。
- loss32: Wine の上の Win32 のソフトウェアだけでデスクトップを作る Linux ディストリビューションの計画です。 ReactOS の部品も使います。win4wine が XP 本物のシェルを Debian の上で動かすのに対し、loss32 は自由なソフトウェアだけで作ります。
- Windows 由来のバイナリには手を加えません。違いは Wine とその周辺で吸収します。
- Microsoft のバイナリを逆アセンブルしません。挙動は公開 API と、実際の XP の上で動かす自作のプローブで調べています。
- Microsoft のファイル、取り出したもの、Wine の prefix は、Git 管理外の localres/ と .local/ にだけ置きます。
- AshesTom さん（フォーク）: XP の画面のプロパティ、
サウンド、キーボードの配列、通知領域の XP のアイコン、スタートメニューの左の列、Internet Explorer 6 と Windows Media Player 9、
起動中のようこそ画面、タイトルバーのアニメーションと小さいアイコン、Arch Linux への対応、xp.sh など。
LGPL-2.1-or-later（Wine と同じ）です。対象はこのリポジトリのコードとパッチだけです。
ただし wayland/patches/labwc/ は labwc と同じ GPL-2.0-only、wayland/patches/wlroots/ は wlroots と同じ MIT です。
Windows XP と Windows 7 のファイルと、スクリーンショットに写っている XP と Windows 7 の画面の著作権は Microsoft にあります。
ReactOS のシェルで使う ReactOS のファイルは、ReactOS のライセンス（GPL-2.0-or-later、DLL の多くは LGPL-2.1-or-later）に従います。
