articles.title: Show HN: Hermit CRM – Free open-source CRM for solopreneurs
articles.body:
A CRM for one.
A free, open-source CRM for founders, freelancers and anyone doing their own sales. Your companies, contacts, pipeline, tasks, outreach and dashboards are plain text files on your laptop. Write your own outreach or let your AI draft it, and ask it to reshape Hermit CRM to fit how you work.
- Download it.Download for Mac and Linux Use your AI coding tool to install it: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build or another. No AI coding tool yet? Install it by hand. On a phone? Email yourself the link and open it on your Mac or Linux computer.
- Unpack it and open the folder in your AI coding tool.
- Send your AI this message:
What it does
Feature overview.
Each tile is a page of Hermit CRM, shown as it looks on made-up demo data. Open one to see what it does, with screenshots of the real app.
- HomeWhat is due this week, the replies you owe and last month’s numbers, on one page.
- PipelineA board from prospect to won, plus a follow-up radar for unanswered threads.
- CalendarOverdue and due-today next steps, a month view, and a brief before each meeting.
- TasksEvery task for every company in one list, with date buttons, filters and your own task types.
- CompaniesSort and filter companies, with one timeline per company of every email, call, note and meeting.
- ContactsEvery person across your companies, with a page of their own: roles, history and tasks.
- MessagesEvery message you sent, with what came of it, so you can see which wording gets answers.
- OutreachResearches a company’s website, drafts a first message or a follow-up in your wording, and waits for your approval.
- LearningWhat the outreach bot learns from your edits and from the replies, as lessons you accept one by one.
- ExtensionTurn the page you are looking at into a company or a contact, from one bookmark.
- ReportsWeekly activity, funnel and conversion, time in stage, and which messages get answers.
- Make it yoursPages of your own with lists, counts and bar charts. Describe one in a sentence, your AI builds it, and you pin it to the sidebar.
- SettingsYour name, mail and calendar capture, backups, fields, deal stages and outcomes, set in the browser.
The idea
One company, one file.
The file behind the Northwind Robotics card:
~/crm/companies/northwind-robotics/company.md
---
name: Northwind Robotics
website: northwind-robotics.com
country: DE
source: referral
stage: offer
stage_changed: 2026-09-15
value_eur_month: 4000
next_step: Follow up on the proposal
next_step_due: 2026-09-24
...
      Adjust
Make it yours, with your own AI.
Say what you want in one sentence. Your own AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Gemini CLI) builds it in your data folder, following recipes that come with Hermit, and you see it on the next page load.
- A dashboard from one sentence You type Make a dashboard called “Monday review” with my open deals, what is due this week and the deals by stage with their value. Pin it to the sidebar. What changes One new file, dashboards/monday-review.toml. The page is pinned in the sidebar, and every number opens the records behind it.
- A new field You type Add a “date” field for “contract renewal” to companies, shown on the company page and in the companies list. What changes Seven lines in fields.toml. The field shows on every company page, and as a column you can sort and filter in the companies list.
- A routine that drafts follow-ups You type Every morning, for people I messaged 7 days ago without a reply, draft a short follow-up. Never send anything. What changes A routine in routines.toml. It starts paused, so you see first who it would pick. Once you turn it on, its drafts wait on Home for you to edit and send yourself.
Safe to try. Every change is a git commit you can undo in one click. Routines only write drafts and start paused. Mail goes out only when you approve it, and sending is off until you turn it on.
Outreach
Write it yourself, or let Hermit draft it. You decide what goes out.
Choose who to contact. Hermit reads what their website says, drafts a short message in your own voice and in their language, and checks it against your rules. You read it, change it and approve it.
- Choose who. A filter such as stage=prospect; country=DE, and how many drafts you want.
- Hermit researches. It reads the company’s website and shows what it found, with the source of each point.
- It drafts. In English, German, Dutch or French. Hermit follows your playbook, and every draft shows the checks it passed.
- You approve. Edit it, approve it, then send it yourself or switch on sending from your own mailbox. Replies that show interest and threads nobody answered get drafts too.
You stay in charge. Nothing is sent that you did not approve, and sending is off until you turn it on. Every step is saved as a version you can undo.
Your data stays with you. Hermit runs on your computer, not in the cloud. Your companies, contacts and notes are ordinary text files in a folder you own, so you can open, copy or back them up like any document. Technically: Markdown files in a git repository.
Your AI does the admin. Use the AI subscription you already have, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. There are no credits to buy from a CRM vendor, and Hermit CRM adds no AI bill. Ask what is in your pipeline this week, or to log a call with a contact, and it reads and updates your records for you. Ask Hermit is a question box on every page: ask who you wrote to last week without a follow-up planned, and your AI tool answers from your own records, with links to the people and companies. It only reads and never changes anything. For developers: plain files, a small command line tool and an MCP server.
Yours to change. Press Adjust on any page and describe what you want: a dashboard, a field, a page layout, a routine. Your AI assistant builds it, every change can be undone, and the code is open source.
Questions
Where does my data live?
In one folder on your computer, ~/crm unless you choose another. Every company, contact and conversation is its own plain text file, and Hermit saves a version each time something changes, so any mistake can be undone. Technically: Markdown files in a git repository, and git revert goes back.
What are Markdown and git?
Markdown is a simple text format that any editor can open, so your records are never locked inside Hermit. Git is a free tool that remembers every version of your files. Hermit uses both so that you can read your data without Hermit and undo any change. You never have to type a git command yourself.
Does anything leave my Mac?
Only what you set up or ask for. Mail you approved, once you turn sending on. A private git backup, if you add one. The AI tool you ask, when you use Ask Hermit, enrichment, routines or outreach drafts. A public web page, when you add a company from its address or let outreach research one. Your mailbox and calendar, if you connect them. And a once-a-day version check with no identifiers, which you can turn off.
Do I need to be a developer?
No, but you do need an AI coding tool such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor to install it, or you can install it by hand with Python and git. Your AI tool runs the commands and tells you in plain words what it is doing. On a fresh Mac you click Install once in an Apple dialog.
Does it run on Linux?
Yes, but it is less tested than on a Mac. The install is the same: your AI tool checks for git and Python and installs what is missing, which on Linux may ask for your password. There is no keychain on Linux, so the mail password is kept in a file only your user account can read.
Which AI tools work?
For the install, any AI coding tool that can read a file and run commands: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and others. Afterwards, Claude Desktop, ChatGPT, Cursor or any other MCP client can read your pipeline and log interactions. An AI tool that wants the whole manual can read the docs, or the same text as one file in llms-full.txt.
Does it work with my email and calendar?
Yes, without OAuth. BCC or forward mail to an address such as you+crm@gmail.com and it is logged on the right contact. Past meetings come in from your calendar’s secret ICS link (Google, Outlook or iCloud). You type the app password and the link into the Settings page yourself, so they never pass through an AI chat.
Can my team use it?
No. Hermit CRM is built for one person. If you need a team CRM, use one of the others.
How does it compare with HubSpot, Attio or Pipedrive?
Those are hosted CRMs for teams, priced per seat, with your data in their cloud. Hermit CRM is free, for one person, and keeps your data on your own computer. Hermit CRM compared puts it side by side with HubSpot, Attio, Pipedrive, folk, Twenty and Notion, and says when each one is the better choice.
Does it run on Windows?
Not yet. Hermit CRM runs on macOS, and on Linux where it is less tested.
What does it cost?
Nothing. It is free and open source under the Apache License 2.0. It comes with no warranty and no support; see DISCLAIMER.md in the download.
Free and open source. Your data stays in a folder on your computer.
Use your AI coding tool to install it.

articles.title: You can't afford to keep your SSH keys on disk
articles.body:
You can't afford to keep your SSH keys on disk
Although it's clear to me that some of the panic is unwarranted, all the recent security vulnerability reports and company breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.
I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them. This has changed in the last couple of months, where I've instead been pruning my running services. I've taken down unused old apps, because anything can be an entry point into your system. And they were unused anyway. I've also moved most of services behind my Tailscale, with some judicious use of tailscale funnel to poke little holes for specific things that do need to be publicly accessible. And I've been obssessively updating everything on my servers that can be updated.
That brings us to my personal computer. I've been trying to do the same kind of due diligence that I did for my servers, on my personal devices. I have been a long time user of password managers, and I recently wrote about moving to Bitwarden, and I am careful to always enable 2FA or passkeys on every service I use. But one area I've fallen behind is SSH keys.
A better approach to SSH keys
I was keeping copies of my private keys in my password manager, for safe-keeping, but I was still using the version on disk, loaded into memory with ssh-add. To just make this absolutely clear, this means that the private keys are vulnerable to be exiltrated by malicious code scanning my disk. After reading articles like I deleted all my SSH keys, I finally decided to take the next step and get them off disk.
I knew that for this to work for me, it had to be easy to use and the disruption had to be minimal, and so although things like the OSX Secure Enclave sounds incredibly cool, I needed something with better ergonomics. I already had Bitwarden set up, with the keys in it, and so that's the approach I ended up taking, and it has worked great for me.
Setting up the Bitwarden SSH agent
Ok, let's go through the steps. First, make sure your private keys are in Bitwarden. If they are not, you'll want to import them. Note that the Bitwarden UI for importing SSH keys is a bit awkward.
- Create a new SSH key in Bitwarden, it'll automatically generate one for you.
- Copy your existing private key into your clipboard, eg cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | pbcopy.
- On the Private Key header in the edit form, at the very far right of the asterisks hiding the value, there's an upload icon, click it.
- Your private key has been imported. Give it a good name and save.
Once you're done with that, you can now move on to the next step, which is enabling the Bitwarden SSH agent. Note that these instructions are for the direct install, if you installed it through the App Store I think the path is different. Go to Preferences, App settings (all accounts), and find the checkbox for "Enable SSH agent". You'll also get the option of choosing how often it prompts you for permission, when something wants to use the key. I went for whenever the vault is locked, which I have set to every 4 hours, balancing security with convenience.
Next, add to your ~/.ssh/config file:
Host *
  IdentityAgent ~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock
This tells ssh to use the Bitwarden SSH agent. This applies globally, so anything that calls ssh should now check the agent. Separately, you'll want to add this to your terminal config file, eg .zshrc:
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK=~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock
This ensures anything that needs the SSH agent in your terminal, that isn't ssh, also go to the right place. This covers tools like ssh-keygen. Okay, now try it out with ssh-add -L. This should list all the keys loaded into ssh-agent. If you're confident you've copied all of your keys into your password manager, you can now delete the ones on disk.
Bonus: git commit signing
Git commits traditionally contain author information, but no proof that the author is who they say they are. This means it's trivial to impersonate someone else in a commit. It's still mitigated by the fact that git repositories generally have access controls, so a third party would not be able to push commits in the first place, but there is also a mechanism available for proving that the git originated from the claimed author: commit signing.
In the past, this was limited to GPG keys, but modern git supports signing using SSH keys. So I've set this up too, using a dedicated key that only has that job. This means that creating the commit and pushing it to the repo requires two separate SSH keys, and each one has to be authorized separately.
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey "key::$(ssh-add -L | grep 'YOURKEYNAME')"
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgsign true
Go to a repo and create a commit, then run git cat-file -p HEAD, and you should see your signature there.
To have forges recognize your signature you have to teach them what it is. For Github that means going to https://github.com/settings/keys and adding it as a signing key. Tangled automatically trusts your configured SSH keys as signing keys. Gitea and Forgejo require some extra steps to trust your key, just follow their instructions at /user/settings/keys.
My experience after a couple of weeks
I've adjusted quickly. Everything just works out of the box, the only added friction is that now and then Bitwarden prompts me for permission to use keys, which if it's unlocked just means clicking "approve" on a dialog. If it's locked, I can unlock it with touch ID.
If any Bitwarden employees happen to be reading this, it would be nice if instead of clicking approve, I could use touch ID to approve use of the key. Or at least by hitting enter. As it is, I always have to move to the touchpad to approve. It would also be great if I could separately configure the vault lock interval and the same interval for keys. But that's just minor requests, overall it works just great for me, and it's not too disruptive.
And now I get to sleep a bit easier!
Written by Johanna Larsson. Thoughts on this post? Find me on Bluesky at @jola.dev .
Related posts
Proposal for Tranquil PDS: Type-safe scopes
Tranquil is a popular AT protocol PDS implementation. This is a proposal to introduce a type-safe building block for representing scopes.
Building an atproto account typeahead search service
Tern is a single binary atproto account typeahead, covering both display names and handles, with near instant updates.
Tangled in a box
What if you could run your own Tangled on a private network, behind Tailscale, or locally.

articles.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
articles.body:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.
xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko).
With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.
One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.
The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).
Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto).
Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia): hosted macOS 27 running with
4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark
host into the hosted Darwin userspace.
Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac (Chip: Unknown, 7.80 GB memory, macOS Golden Gate 27.2)
alongside sysctl machdep.cpu (ARM processor, hw.cpufamily: 0, hw.ncpu: 4) and hw.optional.arm.
 macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...)    Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────    ────────────────────────────────────────────
 XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts)  │
   ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)
 xnu.ko   (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)
   ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)
 fki.ko   (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)
 Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)
- CPUs: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of
XNU code to XNU's handlers.
- Memory: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).
- Devices: kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.
- GPU: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
host's GPU through the DRM bridge (kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using
Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.
Working on two arm64 Linux setups:
- Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit, 1 to 6 hosted CPUs):
  - macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).
  - Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.
  - Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/.
  - The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)) and is enabled by default
(GPU=auto) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (GPU=off) otherwise.
- Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia):
  - Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with CPUS=4 and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU.
  - Currently renders on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, GPU=off): xnudrmd only forwards virtio-gpu (Venus) ioctls today,
so hardware GPU pass-through on the GB10 GPU requires a new DRM bridge backend.
What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).
- An arm64 Linux host with PAC (FEAT_PAuth), 4K pages, and at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted
kernel). Tested on:
  - NVIDIA DGX Spark (bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia; CPU rendering for now).
  - Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit for GPU access via virtio-gpu Venus, or tart).
- A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts.
- A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or distributed by it: the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation.
- scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU
(xnu-12377.121.6) natively on arm64.
- scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh: applies xnu-patches/, builds the kernel and kexts/, and links the kernel collection
with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation.
- scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk
and copies it into the Linux VM.
- scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings
up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh, its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py, input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py. On a bare-metal
host (such as a DGX Spark), set the carve-out (mem=, carve_base=, carve_mb=) to fit the machine's physical
memory layout, and set GPU=off (xnudrmd supports only virtio-gpu for now).
- scripts/install-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): runs it as xnulinux.service, configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself
running.
- GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the
Metal plugin (see its README).
The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an
SPDX-License-Identifier; the license texts are in LICENSES/.
xnu.ko is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and
Linux reports it as a non-GPL module (MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary"), which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not
include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than fki_*, or carry Linux code. Upstream code
(XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at
build time; it is never committed.
- macOS-DroidVM and UniXNU: the 4K-page XNU base, the Linux-hosted XNU toolchain, and the display, Ethernet and input kexts these are derived from.
- metal2vulkan, Mesa (Venus, lavapipe), virglrenderer and krunkit.

articles.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
articles.body:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.
xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko).
With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.
One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.
The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).
Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto).
Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia): hosted macOS 27 running with
4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark
host into the hosted Darwin userspace.
Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac (Chip: Unknown, 7.80 GB memory, macOS Golden Gate 27.2)
alongside sysctl machdep.cpu (ARM processor, hw.cpufamily: 0, hw.ncpu: 4) and hw.optional.arm.
 macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...)    Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────    ────────────────────────────────────────────
 XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts)  │
   ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)
 xnu.ko   (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)
   ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)
 fki.ko   (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)
 Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)
- CPUs: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of
XNU code to XNU's handlers.
- Memory: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).
- Devices: kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.
- GPU: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
host's GPU through the DRM bridge (kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using
Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.
Working on two arm64 Linux setups:
- Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit, 1 to 6 hosted CPUs):
  - macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).
  - Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.
  - Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/.
  - The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)) and is enabled by default
(GPU=auto) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (GPU=off) otherwise.
- Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia):
  - Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with CPUS=4 and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU.
  - Currently renders on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, GPU=off): xnudrmd only forwards virtio-gpu (Venus) ioctls today,
so hardware GPU pass-through on the GB10 GPU requires a new DRM bridge backend.
What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).
- An arm64 Linux host with PAC (FEAT_PAuth), 4K pages, and at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted
kernel). Tested on:
  - NVIDIA DGX Spark (bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia; CPU rendering for now).
  - Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit for GPU access via virtio-gpu Venus, or tart).
- A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts.
- A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or distributed by it: the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation.
- scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU
(xnu-12377.121.6) natively on arm64.
- scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh: applies xnu-patches/, builds the kernel and kexts/, and links the kernel collection
with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation.
- scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk
and copies it into the Linux VM.
- scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings
up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh, its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py, input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py. On a bare-metal
host (such as a DGX Spark), set the carve-out (mem=, carve_base=, carve_mb=) to fit the machine's physical
memory layout, and set GPU=off (xnudrmd supports only virtio-gpu for now).
- scripts/install-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): runs it as xnulinux.service, configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself
running.
- GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the
Metal plugin (see its README).
The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an

articles.title: Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after "input from senior levels of the United States government"
articles.body: Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after "input from senior levels of the United States government"

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he’ll be a ‘better CEO’ as staff applauds his return
articles.body:
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s office as CEO today to a crowd of applauding employees who stood and filmed the cofounder’s first moments back.
Jensen Huang says he’ll be a ‘better CEO’ as staff applauds his return
Nvidia’s reinstated CEO thanked employees for the ‘second chances.’
“Thank you all for the second chances. I’m gonna be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang said, as shown in a video of his return.
Huang resigned as CEO on November 12th following reports of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a direct report at Nvidia. Huang admitted two days before that he was “unfaithful to my wife.”
President Trump, who had advocated for Huang to be reinstated ahead of it actually happening, was “totally involved” in his return, the White House said. In its press release about Huang’s reinstatement, the board of directors said it “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made it “confident” that Huang’s reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to help with the reinstatement over the weekend, including assisting the board to get “the assurances it needed,” The New York Times reported.
“This is my first day at work,” Huang told staff today, according to a video reported on by Business Insider. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this.”

articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
Zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.
CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.
In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.
The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

articles.title: Google Is Finally Retiring the Nest App Early Next Year
articles.body:
Google Is Finally Retiring the Nest App Early Next Year (engadget.com) 11
			
		 	
				Google is shutting down its 15-year-old Nest app on January 25, 2027, requiring users to switch to Google Home to remotely control their smart home devices and receive notifications. "Then, on August 2, the company will retire Google Assistant on smart speakers and displays, with Gemini replacing the older tech for voice controls," reports Engadget. From the report:  If you've yet to migrate your Nest devices to the Google Home app, the company says your existing settings and schedules will transfer over automatically. The only thing you need to manually move over are any custom clips you might have saved over the years. You can do this by visiting the Nest website before January 25 and clicking the "Download all" button. Google says it will automatically migrate Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to its newer Google Home Premium package. "You will receive an email closer to the date of transfer detailing your subscription information," the company adds.  "The Nest app launched over 15 years ago, and home technology has changed a lot since then," Google says of the decision. "To give every Nest user Google's latest security protections and most advanced cyber defenses, plus new features from Gemini, we're bringing all Nest devices together in the Google Home app."

articles.title: And Now Once More My Travels Have Ended
articles.body:
And Now Once More My Travels Have Ended
Posted on November 23, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 8 Comments
After three weeks of being on the road with only a limited amount of time home, I have no more business travel for the rest of 2026. I’m going the spend most of the rest of the year in a bathrobe, blanket over me, cat on my lap, probably watching movies. You know, as one does for the holidays.
If I saw you on the road this November, thank you for coming out to see me and for supporting my weird little monster book. I really appreciate both. And I hope the rest of your 2026 is also restful and enjoyable.
PS. I am in fact writing this in a bathrobe with a cat laying on me. She is blocking my view of the keyboard. Please excuse any errors.
— JS

articles.title: Nvidia employees greet Jensen Huang like a hero as he returns to company’s HQ
articles.body:
Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s offices on Monday to an applauding crowd of hundreds of employees, according to several videos circulating online.
The embattled Nvidia founder had stepped down earlier this month amid a series of scandals — including an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has triggered multiple Congressional hearings over national security, and two affairs with Nvidia employees — but was reinstated as CEO after pushback from the tech community and an intervention by President Donald Trump.
After basking in chants of his name, Huang briefly addressed the crowd.
“Thank you all for the second chance,” he said. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”
Over 200,000 people, including around 10,000 current Nvidia employees, had signed an open letter advocating for Huang’s return. Other tech leaders also pushed for Huang’s reinstatement, including Elon Musk, who said last week at the DealBook Summit that letting Huang go is like “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.”
Amid this increased scrutiny, however, other reports have depicted a different side to Nvidia’s top exec — one where Jensen is not seen as a beloved leader, but as a brutal bully. Based on decades of court documents and over a dozen interviews with current and former Nvidia employees, The New York Times reported that Huang “used humiliation as a tool” and verbally belittled staff at times.

articles.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
articles.body:
Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot
AI disclosure: I wrote all text here, but used Agent Duel (an open source battle system on top of OpenCode) to research sources of Lean proofs and generate charts.
The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?
To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.
(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)
Famous theorems in Mathlib
Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.
These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.
Every Lean package on Reservoir
Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:
- 88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.
- 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.
- 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.
So yes, 17m lines is a lot.

articles.title: Google alternative Kagi launches an email service
articles.body:
Kagi, which already offers a paid alternative to Google Search and its own Orion browser as a rival to Chrome, is taking on another Google service: Gmail. Today, Kagi announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, a new email service that has “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.”
Google alternative Kagi launches an email service
Kagi Mail is launching in public beta with a 60-day free trial.
With Kagi Mail, you get an @kagimail.com address, but the service also supports unlimited aliases and domains. It also offers 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar. On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren’t expected to arrive until Q3 2027.
“Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once,” Kagi says. “There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.”
Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial before you have to pay $99 per year. The service is available as part of a $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription.

articles.title: Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now
articles.body:
Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.
Claude AI can review pull requests and ship fixes on its own now
Anthropic is bringing new AI tools to software engineers with Claude Ship.
Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.
PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

articles.title: My trusty 27-inch Alienware QD-OLED gaming monitor is just $280
articles.body:
Alienware’s AW2726DM QD-OLED gaming monitor was a great deal even at its original $349.99 price. The low price and impressive specs were enough to convince me to get one at launch, and I’m glad that I did. I’m a little jealous that you have the opportunity to save $70 on the monitor I’ve been using for work and play for several months. Best Buy and Dell are selling the 27-inch 1440p monitor for $279.99 ahead of Black Friday.
My trusty 27-inch Alienware QD-OLED gaming monitor is just $280
The 1440p 240Hz panel looks and performs like a monitor that’s hundreds more.
Alienware AW2726DM QD-OLED monitor
If you’re on a tight budget, but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on.
The AW2726DM has more features than other similarly-priced monitors that I was comparing it to, and that still holds true when comparing it to more modern models. It has a 1440p QD-OLED screen that delivers tremendous contrast and deep blacks, and its 240Hz refresh rate provides a high ceiling for my graphics card to deliver fast frames. It’s equipped with HDMI and DisplayPort inputs, and really one of its only flaws is that it lacks USB-C video support. The monitor works great for PC games, as well as console titles. I think it’d be a sweet gift to yourself or to a gamer in your life this holiday.
